name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

name: evio (Go epoll/kqueue event loop; Redis clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis 4.0.2 (C, single-threaded ae event loop on epoll) answering PING_INLINE; the same table also holds Go net/http, fasthttp and a Go net echo server, which are Go baselines and not counted here
workload: redis-benchmark -t ping_inline -q -c 50 -n 1000000 with pipeline depth 1, 8 and 16 against the real redis-server and against the evio example Redis clone (examples/redis-server/main.go), both started with GOMAXPROCS=1 on localhost.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, evio Redis clone vs real Redis 4.0.2 (benchmarks/out/redis{1,8,16}.txt, final redis-benchmark line): pipeline 1: 177,147.92 vs 176,991.14 (parity); pipeline 8: 1,285,347.00 vs 878,734.62 (about 1.46x, derived from page data); pipeline 16: 2,123,142.25 vs 879,507.50 (about 2.41x, derived from page data). The README itself only shows chart images and states the goal 'performs on par with Redis and Haproxy'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go version not recorded (2017 snapshot, plain go build in benchmarks/bench-redis.sh). The Redis 4.0.2 build and its flags are not stated; the log shows a default config with transparent-huge-pages and overcommit warnings.
hardware: EC2 c4.xlarge instance (CPU model not named in the repo), client and server on localhost over IPv4; run on 2017-11-04 per the log timestamps
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement for Go net or net/http (the README says so). Handlers run inside the event-loop goroutines and must not block. Linux epoll and BSD/macOS kqueue only, with a net-package fallback elsewhere. Calling it from C++ means a separate Go process.
caveats: The two servers do different amounts of work: the evio example is a tiny Redis-protocol clone (PING, ECHO, GET, SET, DEL, FLUSHDB, QUIT, SHUTDOWN, WAKE) over a Go map with an RWMutex, with no persistence, expiry, replication, statistics or the full command table, so this is not a like-for-like win over Redis. At pipeline depth 1 both are client-bound and equal. Real Redis stays at about 878k requests per second at depth 8 and depth 16 while the clone keeps climbing, and the repo gives no explanation. Only PING_INLINE was benchmarked. One run per cell, no variance, benchmark client shares the 4-vCPU instance with the server. Redis 4.0.2 is from 2017 and the flags and compiler for it are unstated. The README gives no mechanism and no table: it shows chart PNGs, so the numbers here come from the raw benchmarks/out/*.txt files in the repo. Latest two commits are README edits (2026-05-12, 2026-05-19) and the one before is from 2022-05-14.
found_via: GitHub: grepped raw READMEs of Go event-loop frameworks (tidwall/evio, panjf2000/gnet) for libuv/Redis/C comparisons; opened tidwall/evio README, benchmarks/README.md, benchmarks/bench-redis.sh, benchmarks/out/redis1.txt, redis8.txt, redis16.txt, examples/redis-server/main.go and the commits page.

name: Go net TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is faster than Go
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Go 35.6 s vs libuv 43.6 s for the same echo run (about 1.22x less wall time, derived from page data). Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 1.21x faster than Go (derived from page data). Doc text: 'Go did surprise me: faster than nodejs and libuv!'
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go server (benchmarks/go/echo_server_direct.go) calls runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1), one goroutine per connection, 1024-byte buffer; Go version and build flags not stated. libuv build flags not stated.
stars_or_usage: 139.2k stars (golang/go); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Go brings a garbage-collected runtime and goroutine scheduler with its own netpoller; calling Go from C++ goes through cgo or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart that the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' shows; the rendered chart image itself was not viewed. Machine is only described as 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms): no CPU model, no OS, no compiler or Rust/Go versions, no flags, one run, no variance. The author is the Boost.Redis (C++) author, not a maintainer of the tested runtime. The libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example (malloc of a read buffer and of a write request for every message), so it is an untuned C baseline. The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with an unsafe-IO hint, Tokio current_thread runtime, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The doc page says the author expected libuv to perform like Asio and Tokio and was surprised by the Go result; it offers no explanation of the gap. The win is only over libuv (untuned C example); Go loses to Boost.Asio in the same suite.
found_via: WebSearch: 'tokio vs boost asio benchmark echo server rust faster than C++ github' surfaced the Boost.Redis benchmark page; opened benchmarks.tex, doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc and benchmarks/go/echo_server_direct.go via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Lingua Franca (reactor language, C++ runtime) on the Savina actor benchmarks vs CAF
language: Lingua Franca (code generator targeting C++ and C)
baseline: CAF (C++ Actor Framework) running the same Savina benchmarks; Akka (JVM) is the second baseline
workload: Savina actor benchmark suite ported to Lingua Franca reactors (micro-benchmarks such as Ping Pong, Thread Ring, Counting, Fork Join, Big, Chameneos plus concurrency and parallelism benchmarks), execution time at a given number of worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Not on any page opened. From the abstract of the ACM TACO 2023 paper 'High-Performance Deterministic Concurrency using Lingua Franca', seen only as web search snippets (arXiv, ACM and mirrors were blocked): LF is about 1.42x faster than CAF and about 1.85-1.86x faster than Akka over the Savina suite at 20 threads, with LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring, ahead on Fork Join and Chameneos, and roughly on par on the parallelism benchmarks.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (lingua-franca); benchmark repo lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca has 4 stars
tradeoffs: Programs are written in the LF language and compiled by a code generator, so adopting it means a new toolchain; the generated runtime is C or C++, so this is a coordination-language and scheduler claim, not a claim that non-C/C++ machine code is faster. Deterministic semantics restrict some actor patterns (logical time, reactors).
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the paper and its artifact data were not opened, so tier C. The public benchmark repo (lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca, last commit 2026-09-20) holds the LF, Akka and CAF sources (README names CAF 0.16.5 and a patched lf-lang/savina fork) and a runner, but no result tables, no CPU model and no compiler flags; one search snippet quoted CAF 17.6, Akka 2.6.17 and an Intel i9-10900K for the paper, which conflicts with the README's CAF 0.16.5 and could not be checked. The paper's own authors built the LF side and the CAF side of the comparison. The runtime behind the win is C++, so a hand-tuned C++ actor program could probably match it; the paper also reports LF losing to CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring and to Akka on Counting and Big (snippet).

name: Pony actor mailbox performance (100,000,000 messages) vs CAF and Charm++
baseline: CAF 0.13 (C++ Actor Framework); Charm++ 6.6.1 (C++) is in the same chart
workload: Mailbox performance benchmark: 100,000,000 messages passed between actors, plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against the number of physical cores (1-32), and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
claimed_speedup: Read off the chart (approximate, ratios derived from page data): Pony 0.1.5 about 3.7 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.56 at 1 core (about 6.6x); about 1.67 versus 0.27 at 16 cores (about 6x); about 1.62 versus 0.19 at 32 physical cores (about 8.5x). Charm++ 6.6.1 stays below 0.1 beyond 2 cores; Erlang OTP 17 and Scala/Akka fall under 0.1 beyond about 14 cores. The hyper-threaded chart (4-64 threads) shows the same ordering, Pony about 1.5 against CAF about 0.15-0.2 at 64 threads.
tradeoffs: Pony is a separate language and runtime (actors with per-actor heaps, reference capabilities, no shared mutable state); using it from C++ means FFI or a separate process. Smaller ecosystem and a steeper learning curve than a C++ library such as CAF.
caveats: Charts only: the PDF (6 pages, gnuplot output, file creation date 2015-07-06) has no tables, so every figure here is read off the plot and is approximate. The PDF states no CPU model, compiler, optimisation flags, run count or variance, and does not link the benchmark programs; the y axis is 'speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core', so the ratio to CAF is derived from two plotted lines. The versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka); current Pony is much newer and newer CAF releases exist, so the ratio may not hold today (the qb-vs-others README, opened, names CAF 1.1.0 as current). The charts are first-party material of the Pony project, hosted in the Pony website repository, so the competitor builds are not independently tuned. The same PDF shows a loss: on 'Creating 1,048,576 actors' CAF 0.13 overtakes Pony beyond roughly 10 physical cores (about 17x versus about 9x Erlang-on-1-core at 32 cores), so this is a per-benchmark win, not a general win over CAF. www.ponylang.io (which serves this PDF) was blocked here by the egress policy, so the copy in the ponylang-website repository was used; a later Pony 0.26.0 versus CAF 0.16.3 run on 2x Xeon E5-2690 v3 listed on a doc.ic.ac.uk page was seen only as a search snippet and could not be opened, so it is not used.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'actor benchmark Savina Pony vs CAF C++ Actor Framework message passing performance results' led to the Pony benchmarks page; the PDF benchmarks_all.pdf was found in the ponylang/ponylang-website repository (docs/) via curl on raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Rayon vs OpenMP (CMU 15-618 project)
baseline: C++ with OpenMP (and GNU parallel-mode sort) for Mandelbrot, matrix multiplication, sorting and reduction; C++ compiled with GCC per the report
workload: Four shared-memory benchmarks written in Rust+Rayon and C++/OpenMP: Mandelbrot (2048 to 8192 square images), matrix multiplication (1024 and 2048 square), stable and unstable sort of 1M, 10M and 100M random elements (Rayon par_sort vs GNU parallel sort), and sum/sum-of-squares reduction over 500M, 1B and 2B f64; best of three runs, thread counts swept.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, graphs only. Report: Rayon faster than OpenMP for 2048x2048 matrix multiply at every thread count and for stable (merge) sort at higher thread counts; C++ faster for 1024x1024 matmul, for unstable sort at large sizes, for Mandelbrot (Rust within 1% in the multithreaded case) and for reduction. Only quoted timings: serial Mandelbrot 4096x4096 view 1, Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms before the fix and 18758.684 ms after removing the Complex32 overhead.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (report mentions GCC for the C++ side and Clang/LLVM for the Rust side; no optimization flags or versions; Rayon 1.0.3).
tradeoffs: Rayon work stealing adapts to uneven work but pays split and steal overhead; the report finds OpenMP static scheduling faster on reductions and Mandelbrot. Rust refuses to compile unsafe sharing between threads.
caveats: Student course project: results are graphs inside a PDF, no hardware or compiler flags stated, no license file. The Rayon matmul win comes from Rust not vectorizing the inner loop (C++ vectorized it and hit a compute limit at 8 threads) and from par_chunks removing fork-join overhead, so it is not evidence that Rayon is the better scheduler. The sort comparison pits Rust's merge sort and pdqsort-based sort against GNU parallel sort, so the algorithms differ. Rayon 1.0.3 era (2018-2019).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/rayon and github.com/topics/openmp?l=rust (repo description 'Comparison of Multi-threading between C++ and Rust (OpenMP vs Rayon)'); opened repo README, project_docs/15618-Project-Final.pdf and commits.
why_faster: Report: Rayon work stealing balances load and its merge sort was tuned (three merge variants benchmarked); for 2048x2048 matmul the unvectorized Rust inner loop keeps scaling longer and par_chunks avoids fork-join overhead.

name: Redcon (Go Redis-compatible server framework; clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis (C, single-threaded, started as 'redis-server --port 6379 --appendonly no'; version not stated)
workload: redis-benchmark -t set,get -n 10000000 -q -P 512 -c 512 against real Redis and against the Redcon example/clone.go server (in-memory map with an RWMutex; SET, GET, SETNX, DEL, PING, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE), Redcon run single-threaded (GOMAXPROCS=1) and multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, README table: SET 2,018,570.88 (Redcon, one thread) vs 941,265.12 (Redis) = about 2.14x (derived from page data); GET 2,403,846.25 vs 1,189,909.50 = about 2.02x (derived from page data). Multi-threaded Redcon: SET 1,944,390.38 (about 2.07x, derived) and GET 3,993,610.25 (about 3.36x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7 (flags not stated); Redis version and build flags not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 15-inch, 2.8 GHz Intel Core i7 (README), client and server on one laptop
tradeoffs: Go library, so a C++ project would run it as a separate server or sidecar. The clone in the benchmark has none of Redis's persistence, expiry, data structures or replication. Each connection is served by Go's net package with goroutines.
caveats: First-party README numbers from the Go 1.7 era with no Redis version, no compiler, no run count and no variance. The Redis command shown disables the append-only file but not RDB snapshots, so default 'save' rules may have forked the server during a 10M-command SET run (the README says 'no disk persistence' without showing the config); Redis was only run single-threaded. The Go clone implements a handful of commands over a bare map, so the two servers do different work per command. Client, server and OS share one laptop; 512 connections and pipeline depth 512 favour batch throughput over latency. Odd result in the README itself: multi-threaded Redcon SET is slower than single-threaded. No latency numbers. The README names no mechanism for the gap. Redis-vs-Go comparison, not a runtime-level language claim.
found_via: GitHub: grepped raw READMEs of Go server frameworks (tidwall/redcon, evio, gnet, nbio) for Redis/libuv/C++ comparisons; opened github.com/tidwall/redcon, its README benchmark section, example/clone.go and the commits page.

name: ScyllaDB Rust driver (async Tokio CQL driver vs C++ driver)
baseline: ScyllaDB C++ driver (scylladb/cpp-driver, listed as 'cpp-driver' in the chart config; the benchmark README says the old 'cpp' bar was this driver on a single thread); the repo also has a DataStax C++ driver variant
workload: 'Basic' benchmark: 1,000,000 inserts against a local ScyllaDB in Docker with up to 1024 requests in flight (concurrency = 1024), total wall time per driver.
claimed_speedup: generate_chart/config.py: 1,000,000 inserts, concurrency = 1024: scylla-rust-driver 3734 ms vs cpp-driver 5510 ms (about 1.48x less time, derived from page data); gocql 14802 ms and cdrs-tokio 17840 ms in the same file.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README or config; each driver is built inside a Docker image by build.sh (script not read)
stars_or_usage: 689 stars (scylla-rust-driver); benchmark repo cvybhu/rust-driver-benchmarks has 84 commits, last 2022-08-05

name: Tokio (1M concurrent tasks, peak memory)
baseline: Asio C++20 coroutines (awaitable tasks) and concurrencpp
workload: Spawn N concurrent async tasks that wait on a timer and measure peak memory (port of the Rust '1 million concurrent tasks' memory benchmark to C++ coroutine libraries).
claimed_speedup: Peak memory at 1M tasks: tokio 214,136 KB, concurrencpp 605,972 KB, Asio 853,144 KB (about 2.8x and 4.0x less, derived from page data); at 100k tasks: 23,824 vs 61,460 vs 86,652 KB; at 10k: 6,908 vs 7,840 vs 10,244 KB. At 1 task tokio is the largest (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB). Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M.
compiler_and_flags: C++20 with coroutines, compiler not named, CMake Release default, no flags listed; Rust build via cargo (profile unstated)
hardware: Intel i7-8550U (8 threads, about 1.99 GHz), 8 GB RAM, WSL Ubuntu 20.04.6 on Windows 10
tradeoffs: Tokio tasks are stackless futures sized by the compiler, so memory is small per task but not free of heap allocation per spawn; the C++ libraries allocate a coroutine frame per task. The result is about memory only, not throughput or latency.
caveats: Independent hobby replication (4 stars, 6 commits, last commit 2023-06-24), not the tokio authors' benchmark. The README says the original article's methodology was criticised and the author replicated it anyway. Compiler, Asio and concurrencpp versions and flags are unstated; WSL on a laptop CPU, run count not stated. Tokio loses at 1 task. The tokio repo page (opened) makes no comparison to C++ runtimes. Tier C because compiler and flags are missing and the benchmark is a one-person repo.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust async/await versus C++20 coroutines performance evaluation paper benchmark throughput' surfaced Xavorim/cpp_tasks_bench.

name: Tokio async tasks vs Linux kernel threads (context-switch and creation cost, jimblandy/context-switch)
baseline: Linux kernel threads (pthreads, here created through Rust std::thread) running the same 500-stage pipe brigade; no C or C++ program is measured
workload: Context-switch benchmark: 500 tasks connected by pipes pass one byte from first to last (10,000 iterations), with a thread version and a Tokio async version; plus task creation time and resident memory per task.
claimed_speedup: README summary: context switch about 0.2 us between async tasks versus 1.7 us between kernel threads; creating a task about 0.3 us versus about 17 us for a kernel thread (about 57x, derived from page data); memory per task about 0.4 KiB versus about 20 KiB (about 9.5 KiB user plus 10 KiB kernel); 500-task brigade run: async 1.795 ms per iteration (18.19 s elapsed) versus threads 2.657 ms (26.91 s), about 1.5x; 50,000 tasks: 21 MiB versus 466 MiB resident; 250,000 async tasks run, threads stop at about 80,000 on the author's laptop.
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release (Rust version and rustc flags not stated)
hardware: laptop with 4 cores, two-way hyper-threading, 32 GiB RAM (CPU model, kernel and distribution not stated)
tradeoffs: Tokio needs a Rust toolchain and async-colored code; the gain is in cheap tasks, not in raw throughput. The author notes the advantage vanishes when switches are driven by I/O readiness (both about 1.7 us) and that these costs are probably not the limiting factor for most applications.
caveats: Baseline is not C or C++ code: the threaded side is Rust std::thread, which on Linux is a thin wrapper over pthreads and kernel scheduling, so the numbers describe async tasks versus OS threads, and no C or C++ program was measured (the README only mentions C and C++ servers from conversations). The benchmark repo has no licence file, so the benchmark code is not copyable even though Tokio is MIT (usability mixed). Single laptop, no CPU model, no variance across machines, results quoted from one terminal session; the benchmark repo itself was last committed 2024-11-16 (tokio is active, last commit 2026-10-11). The headline advantage disappears when the threaded version is pinned to one core (taskset: 1.709 ms per iteration for threads versus 1.795 ms for async), which the author could not explain. A well-tuned C++ coroutine runtime (Boost.Asio, Boost.Fiber) is not in the comparison. Overlaps the existing Tokio 1M-tasks memory record (same project, different benchmark).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'benchmark C++20 coroutines vs Rust async vs Go goroutines vs Kotlin coroutines context switch spawn cost github results' (github.com only) surfaced jimblandy/context-switch.
why_faster: Async tasks are compiler-sized state machines (a few hundred bytes) scheduled in user space by the Tokio executor, so a task switch avoids a kernel context switch and a kernel stack; the author measures this rather than assuming it.

name: Tokio TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is slightly faster than Tokio
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Tokio 30.7 s vs libuv 43.6 s for the same echo run (about 1.42x less wall time, derived from page data). Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 4% faster than Tokio (derived from page data). Go 35.6 s and Node.js 74.2 s are in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Tokio server uses #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] with tokio 1 (features full) from benchmarks/rust/echo_server_direct; cargo profile not stated. Asio client/server built with CMake C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt); libuv build flags not stated.
stars_or_usage: 33.4k stars (tokio); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Rust async needs the Tokio runtime and a Rust toolchain; the benchmark deliberately uses the single-threaded Tokio runtime to match the single-threaded libuv loop. Calling it from C++ needs FFI or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart that the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' shows; the rendered chart image itself was not viewed. Machine is only described as 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms): no CPU model, no OS, no compiler or Rust/Go versions, no flags, one run, no variance. The author is the Boost.Redis (C++) author, not a maintainer of the tested runtime. The libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example (malloc of a read buffer and of a write request for every message), so it is an untuned C baseline. The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with an unsafe-IO hint, Tokio current_thread runtime, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The doc page says the author expected libuv to perform like Asio and Tokio and was surprised by the Go result; it offers no explanation of the gap. The runtime-level win is only over libuv (untuned C example); Tokio loses to Boost.Asio in the same suite.
found_via: WebSearch: 'tokio vs boost asio benchmark echo server rust faster than C++ github' surfaced the Boost.Redis benchmark page; opened github.com/boostorg/redis benchmarks directory, benchmarks.tex, doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc and the rust/libuv/go/asio sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Embassy (async Rust executor) vs FreeRTOS
baseline: FreeRTOS (C RTOS, used through the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper in an STM32CubeIDE project) on an STM32F446ZE
workload: README claim that async tasks make a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching unnecessary; the linked Tweede Golf 'async vs RTOS showdown' implements the same firmware in Embassy and FreeRTOS on a NUCLEO-F446ZE and (per search-result summaries, blog unreachable) compares interrupt latency, program size and static RAM.
claimed_speedup: README quote: 'It obsoletes the need for a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching, and is faster and smaller than one!' No figures appear on any page that was opened; the blog post that carries them (tweedegolf.nl, async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) could not be reached from this environment.
compiler_and_flags: Rust project (rust/Cargo.toml): opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, embassy from git master of early 2022, nightly features. C project: STM32CubeIDE 1.8.0 .cproject, Release configuration with C optimization -O3 (C++ option -Os), arm-none-eabi toolchain; compiler versions not stated.
hardware: STM32F446ZE (Arm Cortex-M4F) on NUCLEO-F446ZE
tradeoffs: Cooperative async tasks, not preemptive threads: a task that does not yield blocks the others, and priorities work through multiple executors/interrupts. Needs Rust nightly features in the 2022 snapshot; no C++ API.
caveats: Tier D because no number could be read from an opened page; tier could rise to A if the blog's figures are reachable (benchmark code, flags and MCU are public). Search-result summaries of the blog disagree on interrupt latency (one says FreeRTOS wins interrupt latency, another says Embassy wins most metrics but FreeRTOS is slightly faster from interrupt end to thread wake-up) and Hacker News commenters said worst-case latency was not measured. The showdown repo is a Feb 2022 snapshot (3 commits) built on Embassy master of that date, so the result predates four years of Embassy and FreeRTOS changes. A cooperative executor versus a preemptive RTOS is not a like-for-like scheduling comparison. The only repo claim is a README sentence.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Embassy async rust vs FreeRTOS benchmark latency context switch'; opened github.com/embassy-rs/embassy README, github.com/tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown (README, rust/Cargo.toml, c/.cproject, commits).
why_faster: README: async tasks compile into cooperatively scheduled state machines that share one stack, need no per-task stack sizing and no dynamic allocation, so no kernel context switch is paid.

name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and reaches 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache is the bottleneck. Measured on the page (Tiger Lake i5-1135G7): C 0.555 ns/elt for 10k to 1M bytes; CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 5.2-5.9x (derived from page data); native build 0.0526 (10k), 0.0507 (30k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 7-10.6x (derived from page data). Also: selection from a small table 0.04 ns per element versus 0.2 ns, and a 35% advantage on a compiler benchmark.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
hardware: Intel Tiger Lake Core i5-1135G7
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs and the compiler line are on the page so it is reproducible. The C baseline is a simple scalar loop the author took from a Dyalog talk, not hand-vectorized C (a SIMD C version would win; the page says so), the benchmark density of 1/100 is described as not particularly favorable, and the speedup is a best case for BQN primitives. The algorithm is not the same in the strict sense: BQN uses a data-parallel mask and Replicate, C a sequential scan. Page is dated 2023 (gcc 12.2.1, clang 15.0.7) and CBQN has changed since.
found_via: github.com/mlochbaum/BQN docs/implementation listing, page 'Performance in BQN versus C' (versusc.html); CBQN README for licensing; no WebSearch used

name: DiffEqGPU.jl (GPU ensemble ODE solvers in Julia, GPUTsit5) vs MPGOS
baseline: MPGOS (Massively Parallel GPU ODE Solvers), a CUDA C++ ensemble ODE solver library: RK4 (fixed step) and RKCK45 (adaptive), built with nvcc -O3
workload: Lorenz system (3 states, float32), ensemble of 8 to 8,388,608 parameter sets (R from 0 to 21) integrated over t in [0,1] with dt 0.001 on one GPU; fixed-step and adaptive (Julia reltol=abstol=1e-8) variants; wall time per whole ensemble solve in ms.
claimed_speedup: No speedup numbers on the READMEs (DiffEqGPU README: 'See GPUODEBenchmarks for comparison of our GPU solvers against CPUs and GPUs implementation in C++, JAX and PyTorch'). Ratios derived from page data (MPGOS ms / Julia ms), Tesla_V100 unadaptive: 2.118/0.2317 = 9.1x at n=8, 2.208/0.7853 = 2.8x at n=32768, but 94.157/145.317 = 0.65x at n=8,388,608; Tesla_V100 adaptive: 6.9x at n=8, 1.4x at n=131072, 0.70x at n=8,388,608. RTX_5000 unadaptive: 2.5x at n=8 up to 5.4x at n=2,097,152 and 4.8x at n=8,388,608 (886.082 vs 183.920 ms); RTX_5000 adaptive: 0.57x at n=8 (0.144 vs 0.253 ms), 1.08x at n=32768, 2.3x at n=8,388,608.
compiler_and_flags: MPGOS: nvcc -o Lorenz.exe -O3 -std=c++11 --ptxas-options=-v --gpu-architecture=sm_70 -lineinfo -maxrregcount=128 (GPU_ODE_MPGOS/makefile), BlockSize 1024, float precision. Julia: DiffEqGPU.vectorized_solve / vectorized_asolve with GPUTsit5(), CUDA.jl, BenchmarkTools minimum time (GPU_ODE_Julia/bench_lorenz_gpu.jl); Julia and CUDA.jl versions not stated in the files read.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 and RTX 5000 (from the data folder names Tesla_V100 and RTX_5000); host CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (DiffEqGPU.jl); 27 stars (GPUODEBenchmarks); part of the DifferentialEquations.jl ecosystem
tradeoffs: Specialised to many small independent ODEs (one trajectory per GPU thread); not a solver for one large ODE. Needs CUDA.jl (the only backend that the JAX, PyTorch and MPGOS comparison supports). Julia startup and compile time are excluded from the timings.
caveats: Mixed result, not a uniform win: on the V100 Julia is slower than MPGOS for the largest ensembles (0.62x to 0.88x from n=131072 fixed-step and n=524288 adaptive) and on the RTX 5000 adaptive runs it is slower for n<=8192. The algorithms differ: Julia runs the Tsit5 tableau in both modes while MPGOS runs RK4 (fixed) and RKCK45 (adaptive), and MPGOS tolerances are not set in Lorenz.cu, so equal work is not shown. MPGOS is built with --gpu-architecture=sm_70 only, so the RTX 5000 (Turing, sm_75, if it is the Quadro RTX 5000; model not spelled out in the files read) probably ran JIT-compiled PTX; this may inflate the RTX 5000 ratios. The benchmark repo was last committed 2024-01-04, so the data predate current DiffEqGPU.jl versions. MPGOS times use clock() around Solve() plus synchronisation; Julia uses BenchmarkTools minimum over CUDA.@sync, so statistics differ. float32 only. The source states no mechanism for the gap at small n (the MPGOS rows are near 2 ms flat for n<=8192 on V100, which looks like a fixed launch/setup cost). The CMAME 2024 paper (Utkarsh et al., 'Automated translation and accelerated solving of differential equations on multiple GPU platforms') carries the headline claims but was not opened (journal and arXiv blocked), so no paper numbers are quoted. The repo README says the Julia solver lives in DiffEqGPU.jl and GPUODEBenchmarks only holds the scripts and data.
found_via: SciML/DiffEqGPU.jl README 'Benchmarks' section pointing at utkarsh530/GPUODEBenchmarks; data files paper_artifacts/data/{Tesla_V100,RTX_5000}/{CPP,Julia}/*_times_{adaptive,unadaptive}.txt fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Mojo (explicit SIMD) in mojo-analyze: Mandelbrot
baseline: Scalar C Mandelbrot in the same repo (c/mandelbrot.c, clang -O3 -ffp-contract=off, standard library only)
workload: Escape-time Mandelbrot over 800x600 pixels, max 500 iterations, Float64, checksum of per-pixel iteration counts verified equal across all variants; timing of the core computation only, 2 warmups and 7 measured trials, mean reported.
claimed_speedup: ANALYSIS.md Mandelbrot table: Mojo (SIMD) 0.0554 s, C (-O3, scalar) 0.0904 s (1.6x slower), Rust (scalar, release) 0.1114 s (2.0x slower). README: 'Mojo wins the SIMD-heavy Mandelbrot case ... 1.6x faster than C'. The same repo reports C ahead of Mojo on the other four categories (sieve 1.05x, word-frequency 1.6x, CSV aggregation 2.3x, JSON parsing 2.3x).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0: mojo build --fp-mode contract=off benchmarks/mandelbrot/mandelbrot.mojo; C: Apple clang 21, clang -O3 -ffp-contract=off -o dist/mandelbrot-c c/mandelbrot.c (pixi.toml build and build-c tasks); no -march=native, no LTO or PGO.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro, 14 cores, 24 GB RAM, macOS 26.5.2, arm64 (Linux x86_64 and arm64 CI runners are a secondary reference, no C row there yet)
tradeoffs: The Mojo kernel is hand-vectorised (SIMD[DType.float64, 4] with a per-lane active mask and a scalar remainder loop), so it costs more code than the C loop. Mojo needs --fp-mode contract=off here: the default fused-multiply-add contraction changed the checksum by 10 out of about 42.4 million; clang -O3 on this platform shows the same drift unless -ffp-contract=off.
caveats: The comparison is explicitly not same-technique: the repo says Mojo wins 'specifically because it uses SIMD and the C/Rust versions don't' (C and Rust are plain scalar loops that rely on whatever autovectorisation the compiler manages). It therefore measures vectorisation ergonomics, not codegen quality, and a hand-vectorised C or C++ version (intrinsics or compiler vector extensions) would likely close the gap; none is provided. Single machine (arm64, 128-bit NEON), apparently single-author repo with 0 stars, Mojo 1.0.0 toolchain pinned. Same repo shows C ahead on every non-SIMD category.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com): 'Mojo implementation README faster than C++ OR Rust OR numpy benchmark pure Mojo' led to iinoshirozheng/mojo-analyze; README, ANALYSIS.md and pixi.toml read
why_faster: Explicit 4-lane Float64 SIMD with per-lane escape masks in Mojo versus plain scalar loops in C and Rust that depend on autovectorisation (the source's own explanation).

name: Mojo 0.6.0 multi-threaded GEMM in dev0x13/gemm-benchmark-2023
baseline: Eigen 3.4.0 (C++, clang++ -O3 -march=native -fopenmp); also OpenBLAS 0.3.25 and Intel MKL called from C++ and a naive C++ triple loop, all built with clang++ -O3 -march=native
workload: Single-precision (DType.float32) GEMM, 19 problem shapes from 128x128x128 to 1024x2560x1024, GFLOPS, multi-threaded and single-threaded tables; the Mojo code is src/matmul.mojo run with 'mojo matmul.mojo'.
claimed_speedup: No speedup is claimed by the README; the reference tables give GFLOPS. Multi-thread, Mojo ('Swizzled') vs Eigen: 256x1024x4096 835.4 vs 378.8 (2.2x, derived from page data), 256x4096x1024 818.0 vs 428.0 (1.9x), 1024x2560x1024 808.8 vs 437.3 (1.8x), 128x768x3072 814.3 vs 381.2 (2.1x). Versus OpenBLAS the result is mixed: 256x4096x1024 818.0 vs 770.9 and 128x4096x1024 795.0 vs 688.9 (Mojo ahead), 256x1024x4096 835.4 vs 860.6 and 1024x2560x1024 808.8 vs 1126.2 (OpenBLAS ahead). MKL is ahead on every shape (for example 1063.6 vs 835.4 GFLOPS). Mojo loses on small shapes (128x128x128: 24.4 vs Eigen 109.0 vs OpenBLAS 143.6) and the single-thread Mojo ('Vectorized') column is far behind Eigen (10.0 vs 56.0 on 256x1024x4096) and about level with the naive C++ loop (11.0).
compiler_and_flags: C++ baselines: clang++ -O3 -march=native (src/Makefile; -fopenmp for Eigen and OpenBLAS, MKL linked with libiomp5), Ubuntu 22.04 Docker image; single-thread runs set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1. Mojo 0.6.0 via 'mojo matmul.mojo' (no optimization flags given).
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (README says 16 cores; AWS EC2 c5.4xlarge), Ubuntu 22.04
tradeoffs: Mojo 0.6.0 (December 2023) is an early release and the language and its APIs have changed since; installing it needs a Modular auth token. The kernel is float32 only and assumes tile-friendly shapes.
caveats: Numbers come from one machine and one run per cell with no spread reported. Both Mojo tables show 0.0 GFLOPS for 1024x352x512 with no explanation. The README lists MKL 2020.4.304 while the Dockerfile ARG pins MKL 2024.0.0.49673, so the MKL version actually used is unclear. The win over Eigen is partly an Eigen scaling issue (Eigen goes from about 57 GFLOPS single-thread to about 380-440 multi-thread on 16 vCPUs). The README does not claim Mojo is faster, it only publishes the table; this is a reading of that table. The Mojo kernel is Modular's matmul.mojo sample (Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions header) placed in an MIT repo. Mojo is not faster than OpenBLAS or MKL overall.
found_via: WebSearch 'Mojo faster than C++ benchmark github -O3 clang matmul' surfaced dev0x13/gemm-benchmark-2023; opened the repo page, README, Dockerfile, src/Makefile, src/run_benchmark.sh, src/matmul.mojo and the commits page
why_faster: No mechanism in the README. The Mojo sample code (src/matmul.mojo comments) applies SIMD vectorize, parallelize across rows, 2D tiling and a swizzled tile order to a naive matmul; Eigen and OpenBLAS use their own packed GEMM kernels, so the algorithms differ.

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: Matmul time (median over runs, Xeon E-2324G): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, about 2.0x and 1.8x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s, Nim/gcc 3.091 s equal C. BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, Julia with OpenBLAS, Nim Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded here.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D: ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: This is a library-kernel difference, not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm is the same (transpose plus dot products) but the D reduction order differs, so results can differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1). The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'), unlike the BLAS rows which dominate the table. CPU model and flags are stated, but gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the D compilers' LLVM/GCC bases. Time includes allocation and matrix generation.
found_via: Direct read of kostya/benchmarks README Matmul table, matmul.c, matmul.d, common/commands.mk and dlang/phobos std/numeric.d (cross-language shared suite; no WebSearch query)

name: Fortran (gfortran) matmul in plb2
baseline: C (clang 15.0.0, make flags -O3 -fwrapv -flto) 1500x1500 double matmul with the same i-k-j loop order using double** rows
workload: Multiply two 1500x1500 double-precision matrices with triple-nested loops (no BLAS), one of four plb2 tasks; Fortran version uses column-major arrays with j-k-i loops so the inner loop is unit-stride.
claimed_speedup: matmul elapsed seconds on Apple M1: Fortran gfortran 13.2.0 0.51 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, about 6% faster (derived from page data). Other compiled languages on the same row: Rust 0.56, Zig 0.56, Nim 0.56, Swift 0.56, D ldc2 0.57, V 0.57, Julia 0.76, Mojo 1.12. Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 13.2.0 with FFLAGS=-O3 (src/fortran/Makefile); C: clang 15.0.0 with CFLAGS=-O3 -fwrapv -flto (src/c/Makefile)
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (elapsed time, hyperfine)
why_faster: Not stated by the source. Searcher inference only: Fortran dummy arguments may not alias and arrays are contiguous, so gfortran can vectorize the inner loop without alias checks, whereas the C version indexes through double** rows.

caveats: Margin is about 6% on one machine with different compilers (gfortran versus clang) and no -flto/-march flags on the Fortran side; likely within run-to-run noise, so this is a near-tie rather than a clear win. The README says Clang already optimizes the C loop and that 'many other languages cannot'. Mechanism is the searcher's inference, which would cap a claim at C if the verifier cannot confirm it; the reproducible harness and stated compilers and CPU class are why it is kept at B. Elapsed wall time includes process startup.

name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (per search-result summary): up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA code that experts optimized over weeks or months, with 3-4x fewer lines. Results-table rows (labels matched by inference from a garbled extraction): local Laplacian 262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP vs about 62 algorithm + 7 schedule lines, 2.1x faster (secondary summary: 335 ms vs 158 ms); bilateral grid 5.9x faster, 3x shorter.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come from the WebSearch result summary of the PLDI 2013 paper (https://people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf, host not reachable from this environment, so the PDF was not opened); the summarizer itself said the table text was garbled and matched rows by inference, and the abstract's 'up to 5x' disagrees with the 5.9x table row. Baselines are the paper authors' chosen 2012-13 hand-tuned implementations (not -O3 compiled naive code) on 2012 hardware; compiler flags and CPU models not confirmed. The repository does not carry the baselines or the paper's harness, so the claim is not reproducible from the repo alone (tier B, not A). The 'language' here is a C++-embedded DSL, so Halide pipelines are callable directly from C++.

name: Fortran (gfortran) in niklas-heer/speed-comparison: Leibniz pi series
baseline: C (gcc 15.2.0, -O3 -flto -march=native with -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math) and the clang / C++ builds of the same Leibniz loop in the same suite
workload: Single-threaded Leibniz series for pi, 1,000,000,000 terms per run, three recorded runs per target (TimesPerRun in the raw JSON), median wall time.
claimed_speedup: Published snapshot 2026-09-05T193245, combined_results.csv medians in ms: Fortran 90 (gfortran 14.3.0) 141.67 vs C (gcc 15.2.0) 157.9, about 1.11x (derived from page data); vs C++ (g++) 158.78, about 1.12x (derived); vs C (clang 21.1.2) 146.07, about 1.03x (derived); vs C++ (clang++) 143.32, about 1.01x (derived). Min-max ranges: Fortran 141.04-144.35 ms, C++ clang++ 142.74-144.96 ms, C (clang) 143.63-150.61 ms, C (gcc) 155.46-160.78 ms, so the lead over the clang builds is inside the sample range.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 14.3.0 `gfortran leibniz.f90 -o leibniz -Ofast -flto -ffast-math -march=native -mtune=native`. C: gcc 15.2.0 `gcc -O3 -s -flto -march=native -mtune=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math -o leibniz leibniz.c -lm`. C++ clang++ 21.1.2 and C clang 21.1.2 use the same flag set (from docs/history/2026-09-05T193245/raw/*.json).
hardware: AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 4 threads, shared x86-64 VM (runner homelab-argo), kernel 6.18.38-talos
tradeoffs: The suite compares single implementations of one arithmetic loop, not Fortran as a whole. The Fortran loop is written differently from the C loop: it is unrolled by hand to four terms per iteration (src/leibniz.f90), while C/C++ use a one-term loop with an `i & 1` sign trick written to allow vectorisation (src/leibniz.c).
caveats: Evidence would qualify as A (code, compiler versions, flags and CPU model are all public) but the source states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. The margin over the best C/C++ build (clang++ 143.32 ms) is about 1% and inside the three-sample ranges; the suite's own README warns that three samples cannot establish a winner for small differences. Flags are not matched: gfortran is built with -Ofast (includes -ffast-math and -freciprocal-math) while C sets only -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math, and the compiler versions differ (gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0). The suite's accuracy column shows 9.440 correct digits for Fortran vs 9.499 for C and a 12-digit printout for Fortran, consistent with different arithmetic (not verified). Nim (142.43 ms) and Rust SIMD (141.31 ms) are also faster than gcc C in the same snapshot; Nim compiles through gcc, so that gap comes from source form, not language. Explicit-SIMD C++ (AVX2) is slower (290.67 ms). In the earlier snapshot docs/history/2025-12-14T070941 (gfortran 14.2.0) Fortran took 238.94 ms: about 1.06x faster than C (gcc) 253.23 ms (derived from page data) but slower than C++ (clang++) 223.89 ms and level with C (clang) 237.46 ms, so only the lead over gcc-built C is repeatable. The HEAD pipeline/languages.py pins different compiler versions than the snapshot; the snapshot's per-target JSON was used here.

name: ClangJIT (Clang with JIT extensions for C++ templates)
baseline: Ahead-of-time compiled Eigen benchmark (adapted bench/benchmark.cpp) using runtime-sized dynamic matrices, built with the same Clang at -O3 -march=native -ffast-math
workload: Eigen bench/benchmark.cpp adapted: 40,000,000 repeats of small dense matrix operations; AoT runtime-sized matrices versus JIT-instantiated fixed-size matrices for sizes 3, 7 and 16, JIT compile time excluded from the runtime rows.
claimed_speedup: Runtime, 40M repeats, JIT compile time excluded: size 3 JIT 1.0s vs AoT 8.05s; size 7 JIT 8.34s vs AoT 20s; size 16 JIT 35.3s vs AoT 36.2s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT build 3.5s total vs AoT double-only 5.3s and AoT three-float-types-with-dispatch 9.7s.
compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 as stated in the wiki table header; Clang itself built with GCC 8.2.0
hardware: Xeon E5-2699 (exact variant not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs a custom Clang/LLVM fork (not upstream); the program links the compiler infrastructure and compiles templates at run time (JIT start-up cost, memory, requires source or serialized AST available at run time); restrictions on decltype(auto), explicit specializations and pointer arguments listed on the wiki; the WG21 proposal P1609 for [[jit]] has not been adopted.
caveats: The AoT baseline is Eigen with dynamic (runtime-sized) matrices; the wiki's 'single specialization' column (1.01s, 8.45s, 35.1s) shows an AoT build specialized for one known size matches the JIT run time, so the win is over generic AoT code, not over size-specialized AoT code. Win shrinks to 1.03x at size 16. Wiki is first-party and numbers are single runs (no variance given). The paper (arXiv 1904.08555, SC19 P3HPC workshop) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Whether the JIT'd code gets exactly the same -O3 level as the AoT code is assumed from the wiki's flag header. Repository last commit is Dec 2019.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Clang-JIT C++ template instantiation at runtime speedup over ahead-of-time compiled code paper github' surfaced arXiv 1904.08555 and P1609; repo wiki then opened on github.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (matrix dimensions) become template arguments instantiated at run time, so the optimizer sees fixed sizes and can unroll and vectorize; only the sizes actually used are compiled (wiki: 'performance benefits of many AoT specializations, sometimes better, at a low compile-time cost').

name: HotSpot Java Math.sin/% loop vs C libm sin/fmod at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C loop calling libm sin() and fmod() (src/main/c/almost_pseudo_random.c) built with gcc -O3 -lm; the README's 'Clang' row again comes from a gcc build

claimed_speedup: Java 51.235 s vs GCC C 1 m 4.433 s and 'Clang' C 1 m 4.878 s (real time, one run each): about 1.26x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Contributed Go finished in 28.191 s (faster than both), Rust in 1 m 7.944 s.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm with no -ffast-math (build-gcc.sh); compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source level 15, default JVM flags.

why_faster: Author cannot fully explain it and lists hypotheses: HotSpot inlines aggressively after profiling, C math functions come from a library and cannot be inlined, and Java's % operator on doubles may map to better machine code.

why_faster: Author's hypothesis: certain algorithms gain performance just from being expressed with automatic memory management, because the C version pays a malloc and a free per node and per payload while the JVM allocates and reclaims in bulk. The author calls the title provocative, says it applies only to this algorithm, and notes that explicit memory management in C beats the Java version. Script: benchmark/CPU+CUDA/run_benchmarks.jl.

why_faster: Docs, GPU only and hedged: the shared-memory variant 'completely avoids atomic operations on shared memory', which 'seems to speed up things quite a bit and might explain the important gains' over cuFINUFFT. Only one GPU model (H100) and one tolerance (1e-6) were tested, and the Julia compiler version is not stated.

name: OCaml 5.4.1: benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: OCaml 5.4.1 0.865 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.17x faster than C and 1.33x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins). OCaml: ocamlopt -O3 -unsafe -inline 200 -nodynlink monotonic.c (-O3 only has an effect when the compiler was built with flambda; the nixpkgs build's flambda status is not stated).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 89.7 MiB for OCaml vs 33.3 MiB for C; OCaml is slower than C on primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci (4.897 s vs 1.694 s) and strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs are naive per-node malloc/free; an arena or pool allocator in C would beat the runtimes here. The benchmark is 1 of 5 workloads, and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs Java 13.536 s, C# 11.914 s, OCaml 16.233 s; C is faster on Fibonacci, strings and, for Java and OCaml, primes). Managed runtimes keep default settings with JIT warm-up inside the timed region and may use extra GC and JIT threads, so wall time is not CPU time. OCaml's win is modest (1.17x) and rests on a single run; the bump allocation of the minor heap is why the allocation-heavy test favours it, not general code quality.

baseline: C (gcc -O3, java_2_times_faster_than_c.c: malloc/free for every node and every payload)

claimed_speedup: Java 8.569 s vs C 12.800 s (gcc script) and 12.726 s (clang-labelled script, actually gcc): about 1.49x faster (derived from page data). The project title says 'almost 2 times', but its own numbers show about 1.5x. Rust 13.8 s, Go 14.5 s, Node 26.2 s and C# 34.0 s in the same README are not faster than C.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 ... -lm (build-gcc.sh; compiler version not stated). build-clang.sh is labelled clang but also invokes gcc -O3, so both C rows are gcc. Java: java -cp build/classes/java/main with no JVM flags; JVM version not stated (README mentions Java 15).

why_faster: Stated by the author: certain allocation-heavy algorithms gain performance from automatic memory management (no explicit free, generational allocation) and HotSpot's profile-driven inlining; the README says the exact cause is a hypothesis.

name: Julia (no BLAS) matmul with @fastmath @simd ivdep in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc matmul (matmul/matmul.c): transposed-B dot-product triple loop on double**, gcc -O3 -march=native -flto, no -ffast-math
workload: 1500x1500 double matrix multiply (MSIZE 1500) written as plain loops (no BLAS) in each language.
claimed_speedup: Matmul: Julia (no BLAS) 1.113s vs C/gcc 3.034s and C/clang 3.067s (about 2.7x, derived from page data). BLAS-backed rows (Eigen 0.081s, Julia threads:1 0.17s) are a different algorithm class and not the claim.
compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk); clang++ 22.1.8 row also present; runtimes: .NET 10.0.100, Scala 3.8.4, Racket 9.2
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image

caveats: Not an equal-optimization comparison: the Julia loop uses @fastmath and @simd ivdep (permits FP reassociation, vectorization) and an axpy loop order (c[m,n] += a[m,k]*b[k,n]), while the C baseline is a strict-FP dot-product loop built without -ffast-math or restrict, which gcc -O3 cannot vectorize. A C build with -ffast-math (or the same loop order) would likely close most of the gap. The Julia file also uses Threads.@threads, and the thread count used for this row is not stated on the README page. Capped at C for the mismatched optimization level.

baseline: C and C++ (gcc 5.4.1 -O2) calling plusone() in the shared library libnewplus.so through the dynamic linker
workload: Call the C function plusone(int) in a loop 500,000,000 times (while (x < count) x = plusone(x)) and report elapsed milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: Julia 894 ms and 889 ms vs C 1182 ms and 1182 ms (C++ 1182 and 1183 ms) for 500M calls: about 1.3x faster (derived from page data).

hardware: Intel i7-3630QM laptop (4 cores, HT), 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Gain only applies to call-boundary overhead for very small functions.
caveats: Measures foreign-call overhead for a trivial function, not code quality. The C and C++ rows call through the PLT of a shared library, which the FFI/ccall code of the JIT languages avoids; statically linking or LTO-inlining plusone in C would remove the call entirely (agent inference from the Tupfile; the README itself states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C; an HN search snippet reported a commenter attributing a LuaJIT-over-C result to direct calls versus PLT calls, but it did not name this repo). C is compiled -O2, not -O3. Toolchains are from 2018 (julia 0.6.3, luajit 2.0.4, gcc 5.4.1) and only 2 samples are shown. Many other languages in the table are slower than C (Go 37,975 ms, Node 9,163 ms, Java 4,469 ms). Julia 0.6.3 is long obsolete; the Julia hello.jl passes the library path as a constant to ccall.

name: Julia vs C++11 random-walk Monte Carlo (jlapeyre/ranwalk-Julia-vs-Cxx)

baseline: C fprintf loop (c/perf.c printfd: fprintf(f, "%ld %ld\n", i, i+1) to /dev/null) built with gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2
workload: Write 100,000 formatted lines to /dev/null; each language runs the benchmark 5 times internally, the Makefile invokes each script 3 times, and the overall minimum is reported.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 6.26 ms vs C 8.02 ms (0.78x of the C time, about 1.28x faster, derived from page data). Rust 4.17 ms (0.52x) is also faster than C; Julia 10.17 ms (1.27x) and Java 58.74 ms are slower.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2 (the Makefile builds benchmarks/c.csv from the -O2 binary, not -O3), linked with OpenBLAS; LuaJIT 2.1.1703358377 run as 'luajit lua/perf.lua'.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (x86_64); CPU model not stated; single-threaded environment variables set
tradeoffs: The win covers formatted integer output only; LuaJIT needs its runtime and the result excludes start-up.
caveats: Only 1 of the 8 benchmarks goes LuaJIT's way; it is slower than C on the other seven (recursion_fibonacci 5.20x, userfunc_mandelbrot 2.54x, matrix_statistics 2.29x, recursion_quicksort 2.24x, iteration_pi_sum 1.07x, parse_integers 1.21x, matrix_multiply 1.14x). Times are milliseconds measured on a shared CI runner with no CPU model, C built at -O2 not -O3, and the C side's time is dominated by glibc vfprintf, so the gap most likely reflects LuaJIT's own number formatting against glibc (inference; the source states no mechanism, which caps the tier at C). Not a language-level code-generation win.
found_via: GitHub: WebFetch of github.com/topics/language-comparison listed JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks; read the Makefile, c/perf.c, lua/perf.lua and the published results on the gh-pages branch

name: LuaJIT vs C and C++ hash-table word count (spion gist)
baseline: C (hand-written chained hash table, gcc -O3) and C++ (std::unordered_map<string,int> with a custom hash, g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x)
workload: Count occurrences of 19 hard-coded words over 1,000,000 passes in a hash table.
claimed_speedup: Original post: C 0.234 s, C++ 0.321 s, LuaJIT 0.161 s (LuaJIT 2.0x faster than C++, 1.45x faster than C). Author's 2020 rerun: C 0.173 s, C++ 0.36 s, LuaJIT 0.08 s (4.5x faster than C++, 2.2x faster than C). Ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x; gcc 8.3.0, Node v15.12.0 and LuaJIT 2.0.5 named in a 2021 comment; original post states no versions
tradeoffs: Toy workload with a tiny hard-coded dictionary and pre-split words.
caveats: The author warns the benchmark 'has been misleading for a while': hard-coded constants, a small dictionary, no allocation cost. Comments show the C++ side was weak: a reworked C++ version ran 90 ms vs LuaJIT 95 ms (jh3141, 2014) and clang++ gave 71 ms, and a later C version replaced the hash table with a plain array. No hardware stated, no license, no mechanism stated. The newest comment seen is from 2021; the gist's last-edit date was not visible. Included for documentation of a widely cited claim, not as reliable evidence.

name: NativeMinuit.jl (pure-Julia port of C++ Minuit2)
baseline: C++ Minuit2 (ROOT's standalone Minuit2 built through CMake, default Release, C++17) running MIGRAD on the same objectives
workload: Wall time of a full MIGRAD minimization with Strategy(0) on five test objectives: quad_4d, rosenbrock_2d, rosenbrock_10d, gauss_ll_10_1000, gauss_ll_2_100.
claimed_speedup: Julia/C++ time ratios 0.147x (quad_4d: 0.81 us vs 5.50 us), 0.253x (rosenbrock_2d: 9.50 vs 37.62 us), 0.371x (rosenbrock_10d: 58.11 vs 156.62 us), 0.718x (gauss_ll_10_1000: 32.26 vs 44.96 us), 0.888x (gauss_ll_2_100: 20.16 vs 22.71 us): about 1.1x to 6.8x faster (derived from page data). README: 'Faster than C++ Minuit2 on every benchmark in the test corpus'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12 with OpenBLAS 0.3.29, single-threaded BLAS on both sides; C++ side built with benchmark/cpp/CMakeLists.txt (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release, C++17); C++ compiler and exact flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M3
why_faster: Stated by the README: a parametric CostFunction{F} devirtualizes the FCN call site at compile time, whereas C++ Minuit2 pays for shared_ptr ref-counting and ABObj expression-template dispatch.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars; registered in the Julia General registry
tradeoffs: Needs the Julia runtime and JIT warm-up (the README table does not say whether compile time is excluded); a derivative work of Minuit2, so LGPL applies; not a drop-in for C++ callers.
caveats: First-party numbers from the port's author, microsecond-scale runs on toy objectives of 2 to 10 parameters where call and dispatch overhead dominate; the C++ compiler and flags are not stated, and the C++ Minuit2 tree the CMake file expects at reference/Minuit2_cpp is not in the repository listing, so the C++ version is unspecified. The port reimplements the algorithm; the README says its algorithms were 'audited against C++ Minuit2', but the page shows no equal iteration or function-call counts. The stated mechanism (call-site devirtualization) suggests the gain is dispatch and inlining of the user function rather than the numerical core.

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (DifferentialEquations.jl) ODE solvers vs Sundials, ODEPACK and Hairer codes
baseline: Sundials CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (C), ODEPACK lsoda (Fortran) and Hairer dopri5/dop853/odex (Fortran), called through Julia wrappers
workload: Work-precision diagrams (wall time versus error at tolerances 1e-6 to 1e-13) for non-stiff ODEs: Lotka-Volterra, Pleiades and Three-Body.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the pages (plots only). Text: 'Here we see the OrdinaryDiffEq.jl algorithms once again far in the lead' (LotkaVolterra_wpd.md); 'The OrdinaryDiffEq.jl algorithms come out as faster in each case than the ODEInterface algorithms' (Pleiades_wpd.md). SciMLBenchmarks.jl README: ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 'both far less efficient than the Vern methods'; CVODE_Adams and lsoda 'tend to not do very well'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.11.9 (LLVM 16.0.6 ORCJIT, znver2); the C and Fortran baselines come from prebuilt JLL binaries and their build flags are not on the pages
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (SciML CI runner)
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and package precompilation; wins depend on the Verner high-order Runge-Kutta methods and algorithm-specific interpolation that the C and Fortran codes do not provide.
caveats: First-party benchmark (the SciML authors wrote both sides' harness); results are plots, so no speedup number can be quoted from the page. The compared solvers use different algorithms (Verner/Tsit5 RK vs Adams/BDF/Dormand-Prince), so this is partly an algorithm win; wrapped C/Fortran codes are called through Julia with their own callback overhead into the Julia ODE function, which may penalize the baselines. Sundials and ODEPACK are not built from source with stated -O3 flags. Some timing differences on easy problems are described by the benchmark itself as dominated by start-up time.
found_via: Checked SciML/SciMLBenchmarksOutput markdown (NonStiffODE) after the Julia-vs-C++ WebSearch returned only forum threads.
why_faster: Pages credit the Verner methods and algorithm-specific interpolants; Julia specialization of the user's ODE function (FullSpecialize, StaticArrays) is implied by the setup but not argued as the cause.

baseline: Ahead-of-time compiled CUDA/HIP/C++ kernels (typical AoT compilation of the same application)
workload: End-to-end GPU application speedup from specializing kernels at run time on argument values and launch parameters (CGO 2025 paper), including JIT compile overhead.
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x on AMD and 1.78x on NVIDIA end-to-end versus AoT compilation; 1.23x higher average end-to-end speedup than Jitify (from WebSearch snippets of the LLNL newsroom, HPCwire and CGO 2025 program pages; snippet only, the pages themselves were blocked).
hardware: AMD and NVIDIA GPUs (models not confirmed)
stars_or_usage: 54 stars, 397 commits; integrated experimentally in RAJA (per search snippet)
tradeoffs: Links an LLVM-based JIT runtime into the application; compile overhead is paid on first use (mitigated by in-memory and persistent caches); the annotation interface needs Clang to build the application with the Proteus pass.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the paper (CGO 2025, Georgakoudis, Parasyris, Beckingsale, a peer-reviewed venue that would normally be tier B) and the LLNL and HPCwire pages were blocked, and the repo README and docs/index.md carry no benchmark numbers or paper link, so no page with the numbers was opened. 'Up to' maxima are best cases on selected applications; the baseline AoT build flags and GPU models are unknown. Retier to B if the paper can be read.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Proteus portable runtime optimization GPU kernel execution LLVM JIT speedup over ahead-of-time paper LLNL Olympus-HPC'; repo README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (kernel arguments, array contents, launch bounds) become constants so LLVM can fold, unroll and prune kernel code beyond what static compilation can; the README says it uses runtime context to specialize 'and enable optimizations beyond static compilation'.

name: Ripserer.jl (Julia persistent homology) vs Ripser and Cubical Ripser (C++)
baseline: Ripser (C++, master commit 286d369) and Cubical Ripser (C++, commits 6edb9c5 for 2D and a063dac for 3D)
workload: Persistent homology of Vietoris-Rips filtrations (datasets from the Ripser paper and PH-roadmap, parsed as Float32, parse time included) and of cubical image filtrations; minimum of five runs.
claimed_speedup: Docs: 'very close to Ripser, usually within around 30%' and 'on very sparse inputs ... can sometimes outperform Ripser'. Ripserer/Ripser time ratios from the page: Alpha-Rips 0.807 (636 ms vs 789 ms), 0.741 (872 ms vs 1.179 s), 0.744 (56 ms vs 76 ms), 0.942 (5.844 s vs 6.203 s) and 1.058 (49.431 s vs 46.707 s, slower); sparse=true mode 0.993 and 0.998 on o3_1024 and o3_4096, 0.932 on random16, but 1.267 on dragon2000 and 1.304 on fract-r; dense mode is slower on 5 of 6 sets (ratio 1.04 to 1.99, o3_4096 151.5 s vs 76.2 s) with random16 at 0.803. Versus Cubical Ripser: 0.96 on bonsai64 (2.875 s vs 2.996 s), slower elsewhere (up to 2.631).
compiler_and_flags: Ripserer v0.15 (Julia version not stated); Ripser and Cubical Ripser built from the stated master commits, compiler and flags not stated. Code and datasets: github.com/mtsch/RipsererBenchmarks.jl.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i5-4200U @ 1.60GHz and 8 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Uses more memory than Ripser on small inputs (heap includes the Julia runtime, for example 138 MiB vs 33 MiB on alpha_3_sphere_3000) but supports higher-dimensional cubical complexes, critical simplices and representative cycles.

Author's own benchmark on an old dual-core laptop with a 2020-era Ripserer v0.15 and 2020 Ripser commits, so the page may be stale. Ripser build flags are not stated.

name: SymbolicUtils.jl / Symbolics.jl (Julia symbolic engine) vs SymEngine (C++): SciMLBenchmarks SymEngineComparison
baseline: SymEngine v0.12.0 (C++ symbolic library, via SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 and SymEngine_jll)
workload: Ten symbolic workloads adapted from SymEngine's own C++ benchmark suite plus SymbolicUtils-native ones: diff of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50), 15-term Taylor series, trig-product substitution, 10^5-draw random-expression substitution (dense and sparse rule), variable search on shared and unshared expression sets, numeric evaluation of a 10000-deep expression, code-generation init, and the call of the generated function with common-subexpression elimination.
claimed_speedup: SymbolicUtils is faster than SymEngine in 4 of 10 rows (SymEngine s vs SymbolicUtils s): compiled call with CSE 6.93256e-7 vs 3.13135e-7 (2.2x), variable search on dissimilar expressions 4.67036e-4 vs 2.13078e-4 (2.2x), variable search on common subtrees 1.02663e-3 vs 4.89876e-4 (2.1x), substitution of a 10^5-draw expression with a sparse rule 1.10077e-3 vs 5.92595e-4 (1.9x) (ratios derived from page data). SymEngine is faster in the other 6: diff of expand 6.95691e-3 vs 0.332787 (SymbolicUtils 48x slower), eval_double of a 10000-deep expression 0.0116745 vs 0.331982 (28x), codegen init 1.15092e-3 vs 1.34645e-2 (12x), series 1.99123e-3 vs 1.98982e-2 (10x), trig-product substitution 1.478e-5 vs 6.0009e-5 (4.1x), dense-rule substitution 1.13195e-3 vs 3.95472e-3 (3.5x).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13.0 (LLVM 20.1.8, znver2), SymbolicUtils v4.46.6, Symbolics v7.39.2, SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 with the prebuilt SymEngine_jll v0.12.0+0 binary (its compiler and flags are not stated); timings are minimum over samples (Chairmarks). Source: SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd.
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (128 virtual cores), Linux x86_64 CI runner
why_faster: Per the benchmark text: the substitution and search wins use SymbolicUtils' IRStructure acceleration structure, which visits shared subexpressions once; the compiled-call win is a native Julia function produced by Code.toexpr plus eval (JIT compiled), against SymEngine's LambdaRealDoubleVisitor, which the file describes as 'an interpreter over the expression tree'.
tradeoffs: The JIT path pays a large setup cost: codegen init is 12x slower than SymEngine's. Core operations (expand, differentiate, series, deep evaluation) are 10-48x slower than SymEngine in this run.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the Symbolics/SciML maintainers, single run without variance. The file itself says the first workload set 'plays to SymEngine's strengths' and the second set is SymbolicUtils-native; for substitution and search rows the SymbolicUtils column is the faster of two variants (plain and IRStructure-backed). The SymEngine 'variable search' is free_symbols accumulation into a set, not an identical operation. The compiled-call row excludes the 12x higher compile cost. The C++ build flags of SymEngine_jll are not stated, so the baseline's optimisation level is unknown.
found_via: Julia ecosystem candidate; opened SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl benchmarks/Symbolics (github.com tree) and the rendered SciMLBenchmarksOutput markdown on raw.githubusercontent.com (docs.sciml.ai is blocked).
