name: Crystal: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int>, and C using strtok_r with uthash (strdup per new word); both built by g++/gcc 16.0.1 and clang 22.1.8; best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s
workload: Split a large generated text of space-separated lowercase words and count word frequencies in a hash map, then report the most frequent word, the distinct count and a checksum (Etc::Words).
claimed_speedup: Crystal 0.88 s (peak RSS 8.8 MB) vs C++/G++ 1.638 s (-O2 'prod'), C++/G++ -O3 'Fast' 1.651 s, best of all C/C++ configurations 1.587 s (C++/G++/PGO) and C/Clang 1.988 s: about 1.9x, 1.9x, 1.8x and 2.3x faster (derived from page data). Zig 0.91 s, Rust 1.021 s and Go 1.129 s also beat every C/C++ row; the suite's 'Crystal/O3' variant row is much slower at 3.105 s.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (from c/Makefile and cpp/Makefile): headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer; 'Fast' build is -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with thin LTO; 'Unsafe' (-O3 -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) builds also exist. Compilers: clang 22.1.8 and g++/gcc 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Crystal 1.21.1: 'crystal build main.cr --release'; the suite also lists a 'Crystal/O3' variant row.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Code reading (crystal/main.cr, cpp/src/words.cpp, c/src/words.c): the C++ baseline tokenizes with istringstream operator>> and copies each word into a std::string key of a node-based unordered_map; the C baseline strdup's every distinct word into uthash; Crystal splits on ' ' with a block and updates its built-in Hash. Agent inference: a tokenizer and container difference, not code generation.
tradeoffs: Crystal peak RSS 8.8 MB vs 5.3 MB for C and 7.8 MB for C++ in the same run.
caveats: Mostly a library and idiom comparison: a C++ baseline using string_view tokenizing and a flat hash map would likely close the gap, and the C baseline is slowed by per-word allocation. LangArena's own README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tasks between languages; it publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance) and compiles the C/C++ headline rows at -O2 with hardening flags (the -O3 'Fast', LTO, PGO and fast-math rows were also compared here and still lose). This agent selected the row because a non-C/C++ language beats every C and C++ configuration; most other tasks in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
found_via: kostya/LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js parsed for string tasks where a language missing from earlier Etc::Words records beats every Clang/GCC C and C++ row; crystal/main.cr, cpp/src/words.cpp and c/src/words.c read from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: csv-zero (Zig SIMD CSV field iterator)
baseline: zsv (C library, built from src/c/zsv with 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv'; labelled 'zsc (c)' in the result CSV) and lazycsv (C++ header library, g++ -O3 -march=native); Rust simd-csv and csv also measured
workload: Iterate a whole CSV file and count its fields with a 64 KB input buffer (csv-race harness): four real-world files (nfl.csv, worldcitiespop.csv, GTFS mbta stop-times, game.csv) and generated files from about 1 KB to about 9.9 GB, with and without quoting.
claimed_speedup: csv-race result-all.csv wall times, csv-zero vs zsv (C) vs lazycsv (C++): ~32 MB no-quotes 52 col 6.62 ms vs 14.1 ms vs 18.7 ms; ~696 MB 574 ms vs 1.50 s vs 1.25 s; ~3.2 GB no-quotes 603 ms vs 1.32 s vs 1.65 s (Rust simd-csv 870 ms); ~9.9 GB quoted 7.73 s vs 12.7 s vs 12.1 s. On all 10 files csv-zero is the fastest of the 5 parsers; ratios against zsv are 1.36x to 2.61x and against lazycsv 1.08x to 2.85x (derived from page data). csv-zero finishes the four real-world files in 0.78 to 2.86 ms (775 us on nfl.csv vs zsv 1.78 ms), so those rows include process start-up. Independent corroboration: in LangArena CSV::Parse (2026-10-05) the Zig row, which imports csv-zero, takes 0.974 s vs 2.223 s for the best C row (C/Clang) and 2.348 s for C++/Clang++.
compiler_and_flags: csv-race Makefile: Zig 'zig build --release=fast' (README names Zig 0.15.2); zsv 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv' (libzsv's own build flags not stated); lazycsv 'g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native'; Rust 'cargo build --release'. Timed with poop (perf counters) or hyperfine.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U, 30 GB RAM, Linux 6.17.8-arch1-1 (csv-race README)
why_faster: README of csv-zero: SIMD-accelerated scanning, a zero-allocation field iterator that returns slices into one internal buffer, and strict RFC 4180 validation that simplifies fast paths. The author's blog post with details (peymanmo.com) was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 38 stars (csv-zero); companion harness csv-race has 2 stars
tradeoffs: Low-level API: yields fields (with a last-column flag), not records, and allocates nothing; strict RFC 4180 (an unquoted field containing a double quote is an error); no type conversion; Zig 0.15 to 0.17 toolchain churn; a C API exists per the README.
caveats: The harness is written by the csv-zero author and the task only counts fields, so it isolates scanning and says nothing about downstream parsing. The result chart set shows the top five parsers only; result-all.csv holds all five measured here (other csv-race parsers such as csv-parser, rapidcsv and a Go parser are in the Makefile but not in the CSV). The 'zsc (c)' label is the zsv library built via src/c/zsv, whose own compiler flags are not stated, and is linked with -lzsv (static or shared not stated), so tiny-file rows partly measure process start-up cost. Single machine (laptop-class Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U), one table. The csv-zero README claims it outperforms every library in csv-race without numbers; the numbers come from result-all.csv. zsv (C) is already catalogued as a separate entry; this record is about the Zig library.
found_via: Followed from the LangArena Zig dependency list (zig/build.zig.zon, csvzero) to the csv-zero README and the csv-race repo; no search query surfaced it.

name: Go: LangArena Distance::NGram

name: regex (Rust regex crate)
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT) and RE2 (C/C++ regex engines); Hyperscan also measured
workload: rebar curated barometer: about 38 regex search benchmarks (literals, alternations, dates, Unicode classes, bounded repeats, dictionaries, ReDoS-style patterns, noseyparker rules) across many engines; corroborated by the LangArena Etc::LogParser task (13 log-grep patterns over generated web-server log lines).
claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). Compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection computed from the repo's recorded rebar CSVs for 2025-12-19 (derived from repo data, not stated on the page): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 search benchmarks, geometric mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser: Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang) and 0.488 s (gcc), about 1.6x, and vs C++ 0.99 s. Same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C PCRE2 JIT 1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there.
compiler_and_flags: rebar README gives engine versions (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05) but no compiler flags. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release' (opt-level 3), regex 1.12; C side clang 22.1.8 / gcc 16.0.1 with -O2 -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, system PCRE2 with pcre2_jit_compile.
hardware: rebar README does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 78 GB.
why_faster: rebar analysis: finite-automata engines (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA) with SIMD literal prefilters (memchr, Teddy) avoid backtracking and give DFA-speed matching on most patterns; PCRE2 JIT stays faster where JIT-compiled backtracking is cheap (small anchored patterns, capture-heavy cases).
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; the regex engine behind ripgrep and much of the Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around (linear-time guarantee in exchange). Pattern compilation is slower than PCRE2 and RE2. Unicode tables add binary size. Rust API; C++ needs the rure C binding or FFI.
caveats: The rebar summary geometric means are over different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers are like for like; those were derived by me from the repo's recorded CSVs. rebar is written by the regex crate's author and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). Hyperscan beats it overall and PCRE2 JIT wins roughly a third of the benchmarks. rebar README gives no CPU. The LangArena run is independent but its C side builds with -O2 and hand-written glue, and both implementations differ in surrounding code. Template::Regex shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT.

claimed_speedup: Zig 0.52 s vs C++/G++ 0.863 s (prod, -O2), C++/Clang++/PGO 0.822 s (best of all C/C++ rows), C/Clang 1.811 s: about 1.58x faster than the best C/C++ row (derived from page data). Peak RSS 3.4 MB.

The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) variants; all non-instrumentation C and C++ rows were compared here. why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Zig's std.AutoHashMap is an open-addressing table with flat storage, while C++ std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> allocates a node per distinct 4-gram, and the test builds two maps per string pair (this agent's inference from the containers used).
tradeoffs: Flat hash tables use less memory per entry than node-based std::unordered_map.
caveats: Container comparison: a C++ open-addressing map (absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map) would likely close the gap, and the suite only uses std::unordered_map. The C# row of the same test is in the wave jitaot file. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, LTO, PGO and fast-math variants were also compared and the non-C row still wins. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by this agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, which is a tie).

name: A*PA2 (astar-pairwise-aligner)
baseline: Edlib (C++) and BiWFA / WFA2-lib (C) exact global aligners
workload: Exact global pairwise alignment (edit distance) of long DNA sequences, e.g. ONT reads of a human genome with 6% to 11% divergence, plus synthetic sequences.
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'up to 20x speedup over other exact aligners and is competitive with approximate aligners'. Paper abstract as quoted in a WebSearch snippet (WABI 2024, LIPIcs 312, paper page blocked): 19x faster than BiWFA and Edlib on >500 kbp ONT reads at 6% divergence; 5.6x at 11 kbp reads with 11% divergence; 0.81x (slower) on 800 bp reads at 11% divergence; A*PA2-simple is 6x to 8x faster than Edlib for sequences of at least 10 kbp.
why_faster: Per the paper snippet: like Edlib it uses Ukkonen band doubling with Myers bit-packing, adding large blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics from A*PA (a different algorithm, not a language effect).
tradeoffs: Gains only on long, low-divergence inputs; slower than Edlib on short, highly divergent reads. Latest commit message mentions 'latest nightly', so a nightly Rust toolchain may be needed (not confirmed). MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Evaluation harness lives in a separate pa-bench repo.
caveats: Only the 'up to 20x' README sentence was verified on a page I opened; the 19x, 5.6x and 0.81x figures are snippet only from the peer-reviewed paper. CPU and flags not found. Pairwise alignment is on the edge of the string-and-text category.
found_via: WebSearch 'A*PA2 exact global sequence alignment Rust faster than Edlib WFA github astarpa2'; opened the repo page and commits feed.

name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract as returned in a WebSearch snippet (the bioRxiv page itself is blocked here): 4x to 15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp, text throughput near 2 Gbp/s, over 100x faster than parasail, 100x faster than SWOffinder on CRISPR off-target search. Repo README: version 2 is 2x faster on AVX-512 and pre-encoding patterns is 10-20x faster for short texts (these are internal comparisons).
compiler_and_flags: README: build with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' (AVX2 or NEON needed); Edlib build flags not seen.
why_faster: Bit-packing with SIMD (AVX2/NEON) where the bit-vectors run along the text direction ('tiling in the text direction'), with the text split into 4 parts searched in parallel; complexity O(k ceil(n/W)) with W=256.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars; published on crates.io, bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Numbers come from the paper abstract as quoted in a search snippet (snippet only); the preprint, the Bioinformatics article (doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag244, listed on the README) and the eval CSVs were not opened. Edlib uses no explicit SIMD, so the comparison pits AVX2 against a scalar-word Myers implementation. The README itself never states the Edlib ratio. Repository evals/ directory has the harness (run_tool_bench.py) so a reproduction is possible.
found_via: WebSearch 'Sassy SIMD approximate string matching DNA Rust faster than Edlib speedup'; opened README, evals/README.md and repo page.

name: cuniq (Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: GNU coreutils 8.32 `sort -u | wc -l` and `sort | uniq -c`, and GNU awk 5.3.2 (`a[$0]++`), all C programs.
workload: Count distinct lines (and per-line occurrence counts) of a 32 GiB preprocessed Wikipedia text dump with 6,028,206,370 lines, 78,035,032 of them unique; also a 4,000,000-line random-number file in criterion benches.
claimed_speedup: PERFORMANCE.md, 32 GiB test: `sort -u huge.txt | wc -l` 14m11.935s vs `cuniq --memmap --threads=1` 2m47.462s (5.1x, derived from page data), `cuniq --memmap --mode=near-exact` (16 threads) 59.387 s (14.3x, derived), `--mode=estimate` (HyperLogLog, 0.74% error) 9.038 s. Report mode: `sort | uniq -c` 28m46.811s and awk 25m03.082s vs `cuniq --memmap -c` 3m07.817s (9.2x and 8.0x, derived). README: 'For counting cuniq reliably outperforms GNU sort in all cases', with one exception for reports on inputs with almost no duplicates.
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly with `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=std --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (recipe in PERFORMANCE.md, with profile-guided optimization mentioned); GNU tools are prebuilt Windows binaries run from Git Bash, build flags unknown.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (16 threads), 5200 MT/s memory, 6950 MB/s sequential disk read, Windows 11 24H2
why_faster: PERFORMANCE.md optimization list: hash table instead of sorting (O(n)), memory-mapped input, memchr newline search, no UTF-8 validation, ahash, leaking large structures instead of freeing, multithreaded hashing and HyperLogLog for the estimate mode.
stars_or_usage: crates.io and AUR packages (per README); star count not seen
tradeoffs: Exact mode keeps every distinct line in memory; near-exact mode ignores 64-bit hash collisions; estimate mode is approximate; -c output is unsorted unless -s; hashing loses to sorting when nearly every line is unique.
caveats: First-party and Windows-only harness: the GNU baseline is coreutils 8.32 and gawk 5.3.2 under Git Bash, which may be a weaker baseline than a Linux build (sort thread count and flags unknown). The win is an algorithm change (hash versus sort), not a language effect. The author's own table also measures huniq 2.7.0 (6m04.595s count), runiq and sortuniq. GPL licence.

name: cw (Rust wc clone)
baseline: BSD wc (FreeBSD 12 base system) and GNU coreutils 8.30 wc ('gwc'), both C
workload: wc-style counting of lines, words, bytes, UTF-8 characters and maximum line length on a 341,152,640-byte XML file (Dickens_Charles_Pickwick_Papers.xml, size from the README's sample output), a test-utf-8.html file, and a multi-file list run through xargs.
claimed_speedup: README hyperfine-style ratios (cw faster by) vs BSD wc / GNU wc: -l 3.44x / 4.17x; default counts 1.45x / 2.05x; -lL 1.73x / 15.07x; -m 70.36x / 30.21x (test-utf-8.html: 84.74x / 124.21x); -mlL 9.05x / 3.88x; -mLlw 3.15x / 1.35x; multi-file xargs run with --threads=12: 11.55x vs wc and 17.31x vs gwc, and 7.07x vs single-threaded cw, so single-threaded cw is about 1.6x faster than wc and 2.4x faster than gwc on that run (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: README: 'cargo build --release --features runtime-dispatch-simd' for best results (SIMD line and character counting); rustc version not stated; build flags of the FreeBSD wc and of gwc 8.30 not stated.
hardware: FreeBSD 12 on a 2.1 GHz Westmere Xeon (README)
why_faster: README: line counts use the bytecount crate, line-length counts use the memchr crate, the -m fast path counts UTF-8 characters with bytecount, and multi-file input can be counted on several threads; without -m cw works on bytes and ignores the locale.
tradeoffs: Different semantics from POSIX wc: byte counting only unless -m, no locale support, limited multibyte handling (the README lists 'improve multibyte support' and 'possibly implement locale' as future work); no test suite at the time of the README; unmaintained since 2021.
caveats: First-party numbers from one FreeBSD 12 machine in 2020-2021 against GNU coreutils 8.30. The README itself says gwc is pessimised on FreeBSD by the system's weak memchr, so Linux/glibc ratios will be smaller; newer GNU wc releases were not tested. The 70x and 124x -m ratios compare against a locale-aware multibyte path that cw does not implement for general counting. Input files other than the Dickens XML are not included, and the benchmark commands are shown only as hyperfine output. Several rows depend on multi-threading or the optional SIMD feature.

name: fast-float (Rust port of fast_float)
baseline: strtod from the C standard library (also compared: abseil C++, netlib C, fast_float C++)
workload: Parse one decimal string into a 64-bit float; best timing in ns per number on the canada, mesh, uniform, iidi, iei and rec32 datasets.
claimed_speedup: README tables, ns per number, fast-float vs strtod (C): Intel i7-4771 canada 21.58 vs 286.10, uniform 19.36 vs 258.73, mesh 10.70 vs 31.15; Apple M1 canada 14.84 vs 176.13, uniform 11.24 vs 165.43; AMD Rome canada 25.90 vs 123.37, uniform 20.54 vs 101.58, mesh 12.12 vs 65.68 (ratios of roughly 2.9x to 13x across all datasets, derived from page data). README text: 2-8x faster than Rust std FromStr, about 2-3x faster than the nearest competitors, and within noise of the original fast_float C++ library.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.49; crate release profile sets lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1. Compiler and flags for the C and C++ rows are not stated (they come from lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark).
hardware: Intel i7-4771 3.5GHz (macOS), Apple M1 (macOS), AMD Rome (Linux)
why_faster: Direct port of Lemire's fast_float (Eisel-Lemire method): a fast path for inputs with at most 19 significant digits and a slower exact path for longer ones; the C strtod row uses a general arbitrary-precision approach (the second half is this agent's inference, the README names only the fast-path design).
tradeoffs: Parses decimal text to f32/f64 only (no formatting). No dependencies, no_std capable. Repo last committed July 2021 (crate 0.2.0 from January 2021).
caveats: The algorithm is Lemire's, already catalogued as fast_float (C++); the Rust port matches it within noise, so the win over strtod is algorithmic rather than a language advantage. Benchmarks are first-party, the Rust version is 1.49 and compiler flags for the C rows are missing, so the tier is C. The strtod row is whatever libc the machine had: macOS libc on the Intel and M1 rows, and (not stated, presumably glibc) on AMD Rome. Newer Rust standard-library releases may have narrowed the from_str gap (not checked this session). Included mainly as the Rust-side evidence for the algorithm.

name: fastgrep (Rust grep)
baseline: GNU grep 3.12 (C)
workload: Recursive searches over a generated corpus of 200 files x 5,000 lines of Rust-like source (sparse and dense matches, case-insensitive, regex, single 100k-line file) and a scaling test of 50 to 500 files.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (warm trigram index, LC_ALL=C): -rn 'fn main' 8.82 ms vs GNU grep 32.99 ms (3.74x); -rc 'use ' 8.55 ms vs 84.75 ms (9.91x); -rni error 37.49 ms vs 82.57 ms (2.20x); -rn 'impl\s+Drop' 45.24 vs 73.43 (1.62x); very sparse SubscriptionManager 5.41 vs 39.35 (7.28x); single file 3.70 vs 5.21 (1.41x); but -rl 'fn main' 7.50 ms vs GNU grep 7.12 ms (0.95x, GNU grep faster). Scaling: 1.48x at 50 files, 2.43x at 200, 3.08x at 500.
compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9, Rust 1.99.0 release build, Criterion benchmarks; GNU grep 3.12 installed via Homebrew (build flags unknown).
hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 logical CPUs), 32 GB, macOS 27.0.1
why_faster: README: parallel by default across all CPU threads, lazy trigram index that skips non-matching files on repeat searches, SIMD-accelerated literal search.
tradeoffs: Output order is non-deterministic (multi-threaded); deliberate deviations from GNU grep (binary files, long lines). Index cache stored under the OS cache directory and invalidated by mtime and size. Not every GNU grep flag implemented.
caveats: Very new project, first-party numbers. Gains come mostly from 12-thread parallelism and a warm index versus single-threaded GNU grep, not from a faster per-byte scan; the README itself notes --no-index is often faster when the index cannot skip files. Synthetic corpus, small (about 1M lines) so process start-up matters. GNU grep was run on macOS via Homebrew with LC_ALL=C.

compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) variants; all non-instrumentation C and C++ rows were compared here. caveats: Tier capped at C: language-level claim with no mechanism given by the source (the zero-copy-key explanation is this agent's reading of the code). Small margin (18%) on a single run per configuration, so inside typical run-to-run noise for a 0.75 s test; kept only because the algorithm is the same in all languages. Go also loses badly on other text tests in the same suite (Etc::LogParser 30.9 s). LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, LTO, PGO and fast-math variants were also compared and the non-C row still wins. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by this agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, which is a tie).

name: huniq (Rust sort-free uniq)
baseline: `sort | uniq` / `sort -u` and `sort | uniq -c` with GNU sort and GNU uniq (C), awk, GNU datamash (C), and the author's earlier C++ implementation huniq version 1.
workload: Remove duplicate lines (and count occurrences with -c) from data built by repeating /usr/share/dict word lists 1 to 100 times (benchmark.sh).
claimed_speedup: readme.md table (seconds / peak KB): uniq mode, 1 repetition: huniq2-rust 0.26 s vs huniq1-c++ 1.67 s, awk 1.63 s, datamash 1.78 s, `sort | uniq` 7.30 s; 100 repetitions: 43.65 s vs 154.99 s (C++), 239.66 s (awk), 285.94 s (datamash), 1062.07 s (sort | uniq). Count mode, 100 repetitions: 90.80 s vs 150.41 s (C++), 163.13 s (awk), 322.70 s (datamash), 933.67 s (sort | uniq). README: 'beats the C++ implementation by a factor of between 6.5 ... and 3.5', 'compared to sort -u: huniq is around 30 times faster', 'between 5x and 10x faster than sort | uniq -c'. Memory: about 29.5 MB vs 26.2 MB (C++) in uniq mode, 132 MB vs 60 MB in count mode.
compiler_and_flags: `cargo build --release` (Cargo.toml: edition 2018, ahash, bstr, clap); C++ version 1 build flags not stated.
why_faster: README: 'Sorting is slow. By using hash tables/hash sets instead of sorting the input'. Why the Rust rewrite beats the author's C++ version 1 is not explained.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded; holds all distinct lines in memory (README: use datamash for memory efficiency); -c output order is not stable.
caveats: Author-run with no machine, compiler or tool versions stated; benchmark.sh loops until aborted. Inputs are dictionary files repeated N times. The C++ comparator is the author's own earlier tool, so the 3.5x to 6.5x says little about Rust versus C++ in general. Hash versus sort is an algorithm difference. A competitor's table (cuniq PERFORMANCE.md) measured huniq 2.7.0 at 6m04.595s on a 32 GiB file against 14m11.935s for `sort -u | wc -l`.

name: RE# (resharp, Rust derivative-based regex engine)
baseline: PCRE2 (C, through the Rust pcre2 crate 0.2 with jit_if_available(true) per the benchmark source); Rust regex and fancy-regex also measured
workload: find_all over a 1 MiB haystack for 19 common crates.io patterns, is_match latency on single values for 6 anchored validation patterns, plus lookaround scan and validate patterns (criterion benchmark popular-crates.rs).
claimed_speedup: README scan table, resharp vs PCRE2: faster on 13 of 19 patterns, slower on 6 (counted from the table); e.g. \d+ 1.76 GiB/s vs 358.25 MiB/s (5.03x), .* 2.27 GiB/s vs 768.24 MiB/s (3.03x), \d+\.\d+\.\d+ 4.86 GiB/s vs 395.43 MiB/s (12.59x), lookaround (?<="|')\s+(?=[^<>\s]+=) 2.55 GiB/s vs 406.05 MiB/s (6.42x), lookahead validate 21.28 ns vs 65.23 ns (3.07x). PCRE2 is faster on 6 (one more is a tie), e.g. <[^>]+> (2.61 vs 2.09 GiB/s), \$\{([^}]+)\} (10.66 vs 5.63 GiB/s) and (?is)<script[^>]*>.*?</script> (7.08 vs 0.81 GiB/s). Against the regex crate it is ahead on most scan rows but the README says it only matches regex throughput on standard patterns.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README; the criterion example is built through cargo with the pcre2-bench feature (resharp-engine/examples/popular-crates.rs); PCRE2 JIT enabled where available (source comment).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X 8-Core Processor (README)
why_faster: README: a derivative-based, non-backtracking engine built for large alternations, lookarounds and boolean combinations (intersection, complement); on standard patterns it only matches the regex crate. The POPL paper (ACM DOI 10.1145/3704837, 'RE#') was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 188 stars (Rust rewrite); the .NET version resharp-dotnet (258 stars) is already catalogued
tradeoffs: Leftmost-longest instead of leftmost-first match semantics; no capture groups or single-match find (is_match and find_all only); lazy quantifiers are parse errors; large alternations cost memory; capacity or lookahead overflow returns an error.
caveats: First-party table on a hand-picked set of 'popular crates.io patterns' (one row carries an unexplained asterisk); match semantics differ from PCRE2, so match counts are not guaranteed identical; PCRE2 version and compiler flags are not stated and PCRE2 comes through a Rust binding. The .NET sibling resharp-dotnet shows its large wins only over .NET regex, not over C engines. A peer-reviewed paper exists but was not readable here.
found_via: WebSearch 'RE# resharp regex engine .NET derivatives faster than RE2 Rust regex benchmark github ieviev'; README and resharp-engine/examples/popular-crates.rs read from raw.githubusercontent.com

Regex replacement on a ~55 MB JSON: sed -E 11.315 s, sed 11.239 s, sd 0.942 s (~11.93 times faster). 1M lines (~36 MB): sd -A 'foo' 125.6 ms, sed 316.4 ms, default sd (line-by-line) 357.0 ms, so sed is about 1.13x faster than default-mode sd on a literal; regex '(\w+) world': sd -A 254.0 ms, sd default 566.7 ms, sed -E 4432.7 ms (about 7.8x, derived from page data).

GNU sed regex speed depends on locale (UTF-8 vs C), unstated. The README itself calls the syntax examples cherry-picked. sd uses the Rust regex crate while GNU sed uses glibc regex, so large regex gaps are engine differences; literal replacement in default mode is slower than sed.

name: bitdp (compile-time derived bit-parallel alignment kernels)
baseline: edlib (C++), ksw2 extz2_sse (C) and parasail scan16/diag16 (C)
workload: Edit-distance and other linear-gap global alignment of independent DNA pairs (1 kbp and 150 bp sets, real Illumina reads, a 32-guide CRISPR scan of E. coli K-12), measured in GCUPS on one core with every tool's total cost cross-checked.
claimed_speedup: Batched bitdp is faster than edlib, ksw2 and parasail's correct kernels on every DNA workload measured: 35.2 GCUPS against 21.7 (edlib), 2.2 (ksw2) and 5.2 (parasail) for edit distance on 1 kbp pairs with AVX2; margin over edlib shrinks to 15% on real Illumina reads; CRISPR-style scan 0.30 s against 13.3 s for the plain DP. BLOSUM62 is several times slower than parasail.
compiler_and_flags: bitdp built with Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, once with -Dcpu=znver4 (AVX-512, 8 lanes) and once for AVX2; ksw2 commit 289609b built with gcc 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native; edlib and parasail are Ubuntu builds (flags not stated; the Ubuntu parasail has no AVX-512 kernels).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 8840U (Zen 4, AVX-512), Ubuntu under WSL2 (kernel 6.6.114.1), one core, no threading
tradeoffs: Research code, not yet stable; global and search modes with linear gap costs only; at most 32 distinct score differences and 24 substitution costs; compile-time derivation takes seconds to about 15 s (375 MB of compiler memory for BLOSUM62); batched mode needs many independent pairs to fill SIMD lanes.
caveats: Single author, single machine. The comparison is batched SIMD lanes (one alignment per lane) against single-pair tools, a different regime from edlib's per-pair banded algorithm; bitdp reaches only 0.73-1.20 of the closest hand-derived tool BGSA. Library baselines are distro builds. parasail's striped kernels were excluded because they returned wrong costs on some pairs. Headline figures are from the README Speed section; bench/RESULTS.md (also opened) holds the full tables (35.20 vs 21.73 edlib, 2.20 ksw2, 5.19 parasail scan16 on the 5,000-pair 1 kbp set).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=zig topic page
why_faster: Bit-parallel kernel derived at compile time from the recurrence (14 word operations per column for unit edit costs versus 15 for Myers) with one alignment per SIMD lane for independent pairs.

baseline: samtools depth (C, htslib); README table also lists bedtools genomecov (C++) and sambamba depth (D)
workload: Per-base depth on a 30X whole-genome BAM/CRAM with one thread, 500-base window mean depth with three threads, and an exome BAM against 1,195,764 exons.
claimed_speedup: Per-base depth about 2x as fast as samtools depth (BAM: mosdepth 25:23 vs samtools 50:12, relative 1.98; CRAM samtools 1.79x slower); sambamba 5.71x and bedtools 5.31x slower; window depth genome-wide in under 9 minutes of user time with 3 threads (8:44, relative 0.34); exome in 1 minute 38 seconds on one CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Nim with --mm:refc required; build comment in nim.cfg: nim c -a -d:static -d:release mosdepth.nim with htslib built --with-libdeflate. Build flags of samtools and bedtools are not stated.
tradeoffs: Memory is about 32 bits times the longest chromosome (about 1 GB for chr1, against 27 MB for samtools); slower than samtools for small one-off regional queries; no gain past about 4 threads; links htslib (C) for decoding.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper cited by the README, which I did not open (publisher blocked); the table in the README lists no hardware or tool versions. Results date from 2017-2018 era samtools and htslib. mosdepth's default skips samtools-style mate-overlap correction unless enabled, and the accuracy check compared samtools depth defaults against mosdepth without overlap detection. The speedup is algorithmic, not a Nim-versus-C effect.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=nim topic page (brentp/hts-nim ecosystem)
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): Nim and D bioinformatics tools that beat C/C++ tools; github.com/brentp/mosdepth README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: README: depth is kept in an array that is incremented at each read start and decremented at its end, summed cumulatively at output; no extra allocations or objects, whereas samtools depth goes through the pileup machinery.

name: Rust regex crate in mariomka/regex-benchmark vs C PCRE2, C++ Boost.Regex and C++ std::regex

About 4.4x faster than PCRE2 as submitted and 3.1x in the optimized rows (derived from page data).

caveats: Toolchains are from 2021 (rustc 1.51, gcc 7.5, PCRE2 10.36) and the benchmark repo is archived (last commit 2021-10-18; archived 2026-01-28), so current PCRE2 JIT or Rust results may differ. The README notes the input 'isn't the best representative text'. It is not clear that the C PCRE2 'Original' row uses the JIT; the optimized row is about 3x faster. The benchmark repo's page does not show Zig. The same repo's nim-regex row is already catalogued. The mechanism is not stated by the benchmark. The rebar barometer from another search is the stronger evidence for the regex crate.

name: Sassy
baseline: Edlib (C++ bit-parallel edit-distance library)
workload: Approximate (semi-global) search of DNA patterns of length 20 to 1000 in texts of length 50 to 128,000 bp with up to k=3 edits, no reverse complement; 91 pattern/text combinations in evals/data/match_frac_0_k_3.csv.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (edlib_ns / sassy_ns in match_frac_0_k_3.csv): 3.6x to 11.8x, median 8.7x across the 91 rows. Examples: 20 bp pattern in 50 bp text 906 ns vs 241 ns; 1000 bp pattern in 4000 bp text about 10.3x.
compiler_and_flags: Rust: cargo build --release -p evals (evals/README.md); Edlib build flags not stated. Prebuilt Sassy binaries use cargo-multivers for AVX2 and AVX-512.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars; published in Bioinformatics (May 2026, per README)
tradeoffs: Best for short patterns (about 20 to 1000) over ASCII, DNA or IUPAC alphabets; needs AVX2 or NEON for full speed; Rust crate with C, Python, R and DuckDB bindings.
caveats: B rests on the README's citation of the peer-reviewed Bioinformatics paper (not opened); the numbers above are my ratios from the repo's CSV and the CPU is not stated on any page opened. Only the DNA profile without reverse complement was checked (other CSVs exist for other k values). Both tools do different work per match position (Sassy's text-direction tiling), so this is not the same algorithm.
found_via: Search 'Rust SIMD library beats C++ implementation peer-reviewed' led to Ragnar Groot Koerkamp's Rust tools; evals/README.md describes the Sassy vs Edlib eval
why_faster: README: bitpacking and SIMD (AVX2 and NEON) with the main novelty of tiling in the text direction.

name: bzip2z (Zig bzip2 with SA-IS block sorting)
baseline: system bzip2 1.0.8 (C); pbzip2 1.1.13 reported as a third column
workload: Compression and decompression throughput of a 1.0 MB mixed-pattern buffer with the bundled bench-bzip2 tool, 3 iterations, single thread and 16 resolved threads.
claimed_speedup: Single thread: compress 18.64 vs 10.43 MB/s (1.79x), decompress 67.14 vs 69.38 MB/s (0.97x), output 265768 vs 265931 bytes; with threads=auto (16): compress 27.18 vs 10.33 MB/s (2.63x), decompress 68.65 vs 69.16 MB/s (0.99x).
compiler_and_flags: bzip2z: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; system bzip2 1.0.8 and pbzip2 1.1.13 from a Nix dev shell (build flags not stated)
hardware: Apple M4 Max, Darwin 25.3.0 arm64, run 2026-01-15
tradeoffs: Library with C FFI plus a bzip2-compatible CLI; optional multi-stream (pbzip2-style) mode; clean-room rewrite so conformance is the main risk.
caveats: One 1 MB input pattern and three iterations; decompression is parity. The compression win comes from replacing bzip2's block sort with SA-IS, so outputs are not byte-identical to bzip2 and the gain is algorithmic. The threads=auto row adds parallel block compression that stock bzip2 lacks. First-party.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/compression?l=zig topic page
why_faster: README: SA-IS linear-time suffix array construction for the Burrows-Wheeler transform in place of bzip2's original block-sorting logic, plus optional concurrent block compression.

workload: Rendering DjVu pages (colour IW44 page at 150 dpi, bilevel JB2 page at 300 dpi, cold open plus decode plus render) and encoding (IW44 colour scan vs c44, lossless JB2 text page vs cjb2) on checked-in corpus files.

The scorecard fastest rows (map atlas 29.6 ms vs 348.6 ms) differ from the README table rows, which are not in the scorecard. It appears the harness times the external c44 and cjb2 commands (process launch and file I/O included) against an in-process Rust encoder; this was not confirmed in the source. The benchmark dashboard on github.io is blocked here. The README table rows were not re-derived from the raw data. The full-workspace render numbers were rejected once as noisy and re-run, so the render rows come from targeted reruns.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (tsv-filter, tsv-select, tsv-summarize, tsv-join)
baseline: mawk 1.3.3/1.3.4, GNU awk 4.2.1, GNU cut 8.25/8.29, GNU Datamash 1.3 (all C)
workload: April 2018 study on multi-GB TSV files (4.8 GB/7M lines, 2.7 GB/14M lines, 1.7 GB/86M lines): numeric row filter, regex row filter, column selection, join, summary statistics, CSV-to-TSV; times in seconds.

Losses: GNU cut wins narrow column selection (5.60 s vs tsv-select 8.26 s) and xsv (Rust) wins the regex row filter (7.97 s vs 8.80 s).

caveats: First-party study from March 2017, updated April 2018 (old tool versions). The report says tools differ in design goals and are not exact equivalents, and that results are I/O dependent. Compared tools include other Rust and Go programs (xsv, csvtk) that sometimes win. Hardware is not a named CPU model, flags are not listed. The wins over C tools come mostly from awk or cut doing more general work.
found_via: GitHub: eBay/tsv-utils README and docs/Performance.md (QUEUE.md and data/wave12/leads.md named it as a wave 14 lead); not in KNOWN_LIST.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (tsv-filter, tsv-select, tsv-summarize, tsv-join, csv2tsv)
baseline: GNU awk 4.2.1, mawk 1.3.3/1.3.4, GNU cut 8.25/8.29 and GNU Datamash 1.3 (all C)
workload: April 2018 study: seven file-processing tasks on 1.7 to 4.8 GB TSV/CSV files (numeric row filter, regex row filter, column selection, narrow column selection, join, summary statistics, CSV to TSV), 10th percentile of 35 Linux runs.
claimed_speedup: Linux April 2018 (derived ratios from page data): numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 s vs mawk 11.31 s (2.1x) and GNU awk 42.80 s; column selection tsv-select 4.79 s vs mawk 9.51 s and GNU cut 14.46 s (3.0x); summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 s vs GNU Datamash 48.51 s (3.1x). Losses: narrow column selection GNU cut 5.60 s beat tsv-select 8.26 s, and xsv (Rust) beat tsv-filter on the regex row filter (7.97 s vs 8.80 s) while mawk took 17.74 s.

The study itself notes comparisons between individual tools are less meaningful than the overall picture, and the narrow-column test and the regex filter were lost to GNU cut and xsv. Last commit 2021.

name: fd
baseline: GNU find (findutils, C)
workload: Search a home directory (about 750,000 subdirectories and 4 million files, warm disk cache) for the 546 files matching [0-9].jpg; hyperfine means; fd runs with -u so it does the same work as find.
claimed_speedup: fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' 854.8 ms vs find -iregex 19.922 s (README: approximately 23 times faster) and vs find -iname 11.226 s (about 13 times faster).

The speedup mixes multithreading (fd parallelizes traversal, find is single-threaded) with regex-vs-glob matching, so it is not a per-core efficiency win. Benchmark scripts are in sharkdp/fd-benchmarks (opened: README only, scripts not read or run). GNU find was not confirmed to be built at -O3.

GitHub: README of sharkdp/fd (Rust rewrites of C command-line tools); not in KNOWN_LIST.

name: regex (Rust regex crate) as measured in the rebar barometer
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT), RE2 and Hyperscan
metric: throughput (search time); compile time is also reported
workload: rebar curated benchmark groups (literal, literal-alternate, date, ruff-noqa, lexer-veryl, cloud-flare-redos, unicode-character-data, words, aws-keys, bounded-repeat, unstructured-to-json, dictionary, noseyparker, quadratic) over haystacks such as OpenSubtitles text.
claimed_speedup: Search-time geometric mean of speed ratios to the best engine per benchmark (lower is better; 2025-12-19 record): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). Engines ran different benchmark subsets, so these means are not a common-subset comparison. Single rows: sherlock-en 29.4 GB/s rust/regex vs 26.3 pcre2/jit, 12.1 re2, 32.0 hyperscan; sherlock-ru 35.6 GB/s vs 32.8, 768.1 MB/s, 4.3 GB/s; but sherlock-casei-en 10.5 GB/s vs 18.8 pcre2/jit and 29.2 hyperscan.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. Rust engines are release builds by rebar's harness; PCRE2, RE2 and Hyperscan are built by rebar's engine scripts with flags not shown on the pages opened.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K (from record/curated/2025-12-19/lscpu.txt in the rebar repo)
tradeoffs: Linear-time guarantees (no backreferences or lookaround), so it is not a drop-in for PCRE2 features. Compile time is much worse than PCRE2 in rebar (compile-time geometric mean 11.85 vs 1.41 for plain PCRE2 and 6.20 for PCRE2 JIT).

Hyperscan has a better search-time mean (2.37) and wins several rows, and PCRE2 JIT wins the case-insensitive literal rows. The record is close to tier A (public harness, lscpu.txt recorded) but build flags of the C engines were not confirmed, so it is left at C for the verifier to retier. found_via: Looked up the rebar README results after the memchr README pointed at it; rust-lang/regex page says benchmarks moved to rebar
why_faster: The rebar README attributes wins to literal optimizations and prefilters: memchr and the Teddy SIMD multi-substring algorithm (ported out of Hyperscan), lazy DFA, one-pass DFA and a Pike VM fallback selected by a meta engine.

Cycle counts at -O0/-O1/-O2/-O3 are in AdaCore blog posts and a FOSDEM 2022 abstract that were not reachable here (search snippets only; one snippet said SPARK was close at -O1 and a little behind at -O2 in the 2020 baseline, and the FOSDEM abstract was summarized as outperforming TweetNaCl by about 3x). name: verztable
baseline: Abseil, Boost and Ankerl C++ hash tables (README does not name the exact types)
workload: u32, u64 and string keys, sizes 100 to 1M elements, 16 operation mixes (random and sequential insert, reserved insert, update, lookup hit and miss, tombstone, delete, iteration, churn, mixed, read-heavy, write-heavy, zipfian); ns per operation; C++ tables called through FFI.
claimed_speedup: README: 'on average faster than the top C++ hash tables'. BENCHMARKS.md, 100-element u32 set: Reserved Ins. 5 ns vs Abseil 13 / Boost 14 / Ankerl 9; Delete 4 ns vs 13 / 6 / 6; Lookup Miss 1 ns vs 5 / 2 / 3; Tombstone 5 ns vs 16 / 6 / 8. Losses in the same table: Rand. Lookup 3 ns vs Boost 2 ns, Write-Heavy 12 ns vs Ankerl 8 ns.
compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseFast; C++ compiler and flags not stated

caveats: Own harness, no CPU model, C++ build flags missing. The 'std' column in the tables is Zig's std hash map (README: 'Abseil, Boost, Ankerl, and Zig's std hash maps'), not std::unordered_map. Boost wins several lookup rows and Ankerl wins write-heavy rows in the table I read, so 'on average faster' rests on the README's aggregate plots (PNG, not readable). FFI to C++ adds overhead to the baseline. Verstable (C) is the algorithmic inspiration, not a benchmark target; the string fast path (strings up to 8 bytes packed in a u64) is not used by the competitors.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/performance?l=zig description 'faster than the top C++ hash tables'; README and BENCHMARKS.md of ThobiasKnudsen/verztable.
why_faster: README: hash-fragment filtering skips non-matches without touching bucket data; fast path for strings of 8 bytes or fewer; stores full 64-bit hashes for string keys to skip memcmp.

name: Zig (kostya/benchmarks base64)
baseline: Hand-written scalar C base64 (no library), gcc and clang, -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Base64 encode and decode of a 131072-byte string, 8192 tries, into newly allocated buffers; seconds.
claimed_speedup: Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s (about 1.3x and 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Rust 0.842 s is also faster than both. The same table has C/clang with aklomp/base64 at 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7x faster than Zig.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (std.base64); C and C++: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 or clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23 / c++23 -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk)
caveats: No mechanism is given by the source, which caps the tier at C. Zig uses its standard-library base64 while C is a separate hand-written table-driven implementation, so this compares two implementations, and the best C implementation (aklomp SIMD library) is far faster than Zig. The README states no compiler flags in prose; flags were read from common/commands.mk and the base64 Makefile. Values are medians with MAD from one machine.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README tables (cross-language suite named in QUEUE.md section E).
tradeoffs: Single task microbenchmark; Zig std.base64 is scalar.

name: ziggit (Zig git reimplementation)
baseline: git (C) CLI: status, log -20, branch -a, blame
workload: hyperfine (100 runs, 5 warmups) of small git commands in a test repository on macOS arm64, plus in-process library calls versus spawning git as a subprocess for a bun-style workflow.
claimed_speedup: README: 4-10x faster than git on macOS arm64: status 8.1 ms vs 1.0 ms (8.1x), log -20 8.4 vs 1.7 ms (5.0x), branch -a 7.9 vs 1.4 ms (5.6x), blame on a large repo 36 vs 2.8 ms (12.6x); as a library: findCommit 85x (macOS arm64) and 6x (Linux x86_64), cloneBare 7x and 34x, full workflow 10x and 32x.
compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseFast builds (7.5 MB on macOS arm64); git version and build flags not stated; the README links BENCHMARKS.md which I could not open (404 at the default branch path); benchmark sources are in benchmarks/*.zig
hardware: macOS arm64 (CPU model not stated); Linux x86_64 for some library rows
tradeoffs: Drop-in git CLI plus Zig library, WASM build (142 KB), built-in git server and a succinct output mode for LLM use; GPL-2.0; feature parity with git tracked through git's own test suite results.
caveats: Sub-10 ms commands on small repositories are dominated by process start and file-system latency, so the multipliers say little about throughput on large repositories; the library rows measure in-process calls against spawning a subprocess, an overhead difference not an algorithm difference; git version unspecified; first-party.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Zig implementation benchmark faster than C reference library' (github.com results)

name: ZLB (Zig Language Benchmark) Mandelbrot SIMD row
baseline: C Mandelbrot with 4-lane SIMD intrinsics, gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 at -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off (also zig cc)
workload: Mandelbrot set calculation, hyperfine mean of 20 runs after 1 warmup, wall-time ratio against the scalar gcc build (1.00x).
claimed_speedup: Time ratio vs scalar gcc: zig_simd_fast 0.16x and zig_simd_safe 0.18x against c_simd_clang 0.26x, c_simd_gcc 0.27x, rust_simd 0.27x, c_simd_zigcc 0.27x (Zig SIMD about 1.6-1.7x faster than the C SIMD builds); scalar rows are parity (zig_std_fast 1.00x, c_std_gcc 1.00x, c_std_clang 1.02x). Other rows in the same suite: sieve zig_static_bitset_fast 0.63x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x, btree zig_compact_fast 0.19x vs c_arena_gcc 0.21x, log_proc zig_std_fast 0.83x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast (native CPU, README says -mcpu=native); C: gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 with -O3, SIMD C rows add -march=native -ffp-contract=off, scalar C rows use -O3 only (Makefile read); Rust 1.97.1 opt-level=3 with LTO
hardware: Linux 7.1.4-arch; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Informal suite of five small benchmarks (mandel, sieve, btree, log_proc, atomics) in Zig, C, Rust, Go, Python and Bash.
caveats: Not like-for-like: the Zig SIMD kernel uses 8-lane f64 vectors while the C and Rust SIMD kernels use 4-lane intrinsics, scalar C rows lack -march=native while Zig builds natively, and the sieve and btree wins come from different data layouts (bitset, 32-bit indices), not the language. Single commit, single unnamed machine.
found_via: WebSearch: 'written in Zig faster than C library benchmark' (zff.dev mirror of tsukumoakito/zlb), then github.com/topics/benchmark?l=zig
why_faster: Source: Zig's @Vector with 8-lane f64 fills the CPU's execution units better than the 4-lane intrinsics used in C and Rust, and gives LLVM clearer intent.

name: zog (Zig SIMD JSONL search engine)
baseline: jq (C); the README column is labelled jq/jaq and also lists ripgrep
workload: Queries over a 1 GB JSONL dataset (6.7 million lines): key match, substring match, numeric comparison, TSV field extraction, JSON reformatting, aggregation and OR/AND logic, in GB/s.
claimed_speedup: zog (file) 4.03 GB/s simple key match vs 0.07 GB/s for jq/jaq, 2.83 GB/s field extraction vs 0.10, 2.41 GB/s aggregation vs 0.05; 20-50x faster than jq/jaq for typical queries; also faster than ripgrep (2.30 GB/s) and 4.1x faster on complex logic (2.24 vs 0.54 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; jq, jaq and ripgrep versions and flags not stated
hardware: 'modern NVMe SSD' only; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Does not fully parse JSON: byte-level SIMD key scanning in 8 MB blocks with a background reader thread, so malformed JSON and escaped keys may behave differently from jq; narrower query language.
caveats: First-party numbers with no versions, flags or CPU. jq and jaq (Rust) share one column so the C baseline alone is not separable. zog does a different, lighter job than jq (no AST, no validation), so the multiplier compares different semantics.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=zig topic page
why_faster: README: skips building an AST (jq bottlenecks near 0.04 GB/s on it) and scans 32-byte chunks with AVX2/NEON bitmasks while a producer thread reads the next 8 MB block.

name: C# NativeAOT minima-sync (HttpArena entry)

caveats: Comparison numbers exist only as a chart image (Grafana screenshot with no table), so the values above are approximate readings; nginx and Traefik versions and configs, the load generator and the exact duration are not stated for the comparison. The README says the figures reflect 'synthetic performance under optimal conditions'. Its text numbers (129,777 req/s with oha, 107k-110k req/s) come from Aralez-only runs on different hardware and are inconsistent with each other. HAProxy appears only in a feature table, not in any benchmark. The proxy is a layer on Pingora, so a verifier may fold it into the Pingora entry.
found_via: github.com/topics/reverse-proxy?l=rust listed sadoyan/aralez; README 'Aralez, Nginx, Traefik performance benchmark' section and assets/bench.png opened
why_faster: README credits the Pingora engine and Rust ('world-class performance'); no mechanism analysis versus nginx is given.

name: bladebench Rust raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk 8 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s: Rust 49,388 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.21x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (1.50x, derived), ~0 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 and g++ -O2 for C and C++; 'rustc blade_core.rs' with no -O or opt-level flag (default unoptimised build). Not -O3 and not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison: the Rust build has no optimisation flag while C/C++ use -O2, the Rust server binds 127.0.0.1 while the C++ one binds INADDR_ANY, each is a single-threaded accept loop that closes every connection, and the 10 s single-run differences between all four servers are probably dominated by accept/close behaviour and wrk. Compiler versions, CPU and kernel not stated. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise level. Flagged, low-confidence record.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter) returned Synaptechlabs/bladeBench

name: fib
baseline: Sogou workflow (C++ HTTP server) and uSockets (C, BoringSSL) in the lesismal go-*-benchmark repositories; nginx (C) in HttpArena
workload: HTTP/1.1 echo, pipelined, TLS 1.3 echo and WebSocket echo benchmarks, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB payload, GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners with 4 vCPUs (2 for server, 2 for client), single run each.
claimed_speedup: HTTP/1.1 echo: fib 194,671 TPS vs workflow (C++) 150,407 (1.29x, derived from page data), memory 32 MB vs 14 MB; WebSocket echo: fib 138,592 vs uws_events 129,363 (1.07x, derived); README says fib is 'level with or close to' C, C++ and Rust servers; TLS 1.3 echo 103,427 vs uSockets 103,972 (tie).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27, CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' (HttpArena Dockerfile); workflow and uSockets build flags not stated.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner, 4 vCPUs (CPU model stated only for a different benchmark: AMD EPYC 9V74)
tradeoffs: Event-loop networking library for Go that keeps the net/http handler model; no LICENSE file found in the repo, so reference only; uses far more memory than workflow (32 MB vs 14 MB) and TLS 1.3 pipelining uses 180 MB vs 51 MB for uSockets.
caveats: First-party single runs on noisy shared runners (the README says read differences of a few percent as ties). It loses to axum on HTTP/1 echo (236,244 vs 194,671), to uSockets and fnet/uws on WebSocket and TLS pipelining, and the workflow pipeline row is missing. In HttpArena it is slightly behind nginx at baseline-4096 (3,164,504 vs 3,284,513) but far ahead on h2c (12,891,491 at 256 connections vs nginx 2,456,329), where nginx is the only C server compared.
found_via: HttpArena results listing (fib.json, frameworks/fib/meta.json) led to the lesismal/fib README
why_faster: A few event loops wait for I/O readiness and a shared worker pool does the work, so an idle connection costs no goroutine; pipelined requests are batched (README).

name: ioxide
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; also libreactorng and libioma (C, io_uring), mongoose (C) and agensio (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), pipelined and HTTP/2 profiles for a hand-written HTTP/1.1 handler on ioxide, a shared-nothing io_uring runtime for .NET (one ring per reactor thread, raw syscalls without liburing).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,111,381 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.25x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (1.13x), mongoose 3,707,598 (1.11x), agensio 3,558,559 (1.16x). pipelined-4096: 53,376,982 vs nginx 4,037,345 and libreactorng 43,424,448. baseline-h2-1024: 12,235,767 vs nginx 3,320,285 (3.7x).
compiler_and_flags: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7, dotnet publish -c Release (HttpArena frameworks/ioxide/Dockerfile); nginx -O3 -march=native.
hardware: HttpArena dedicated 64-core machine, containers per entry (README says '64-core dedicated hardware'; CPU model, RAM, NIC and kernel not stated)
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring, seccomp must be unconfined), needs a preview .NET 11 runtime; HTTP/3 uses ngtcp2/nghttp3 and TLS uses OpenSSL (C libraries).
caveats: The ioxide repo is owned by the same GitHub account as the HttpArena suite (MDA2AV), so tier is C rather than B even though every entry runs through one public harness. The ioxide Dockerfile notes that moving from .NET 11 preview.6 to preview.7 took baseline-4096 from 4.11M to 3.90M with no change to the entry, so the saved figure depends on the runtime preview. It is behind libreactorng (4,377,377) and libioma (4,255,834), both C, at baseline-4096, behind nginx at limited-conn-4096 (2,543,314 vs 2,626,297), and behind h2o at baseline-h2-1024 (15,633,023). The repo README gives no throughput numbers against C servers. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; competitor rows (nginx, h2o, mongoose, libreactorng, libioma, drogon, cutelyst, hical, agensio) are read from sibling JSON files in the same directory, entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx is a custom C handler module), and the baseline-4096 profile mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model not stated, so not tier A.
found_via: WebSearch 'comparative performance study web frameworks Rust actix-web Go Java Spring C++ Drogon' led to the-benchmarker/web-frameworks; HttpArena (github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena) found by following the TechEmpower-style suites; per-entry JSON in site/data/results opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: One io_uring ring per reactor thread, multishot accept and recv into provided buffer rings, inline continuations, no liburing (engine description in HttpArena meta.json); nginx in the same suite uses epoll.

name: kawipiko
baseline: NGINX (distribution package; configuration in the kawipiko examples/nginx folder), also darkhttpd
workload: Static 'Hello World!' file served from a CDB archive held in memory (kawipiko) or from tmpfs (NGINX), wrk over loopback with keep-alive, 512 to 16384 connections; plus a 250k-file OpenStreetMap tile set at 16384 connections.
claimed_speedup: 512 connections, 2 server threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 req/s vs NGINX 79,816.08 (1.34x, derived from page data); 2048 connections: 100,296.65 vs 78,211.46; 4096: 95,628.34 vs 75,970.82; 16384: 53,548.52 vs 43,909.67. Tile benchmark (i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections): kawipiko 238,499.86 req/s vs NGINX 188,255.32 (1.27x, derived), with ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency and ~25% less CPU per request stated by the author.
compiler_and_flags: Go build of kawipiko (version and flags not stated); NGINX from distribution packages (version and build flags not stated); server run with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i7 3667U (2 physical cores, 4 threads), 8 GiB RAM for the Hello World runs; desktop Intel Core i7 4770 (4 cores, 8 threads), 32 GiB for the tile run; wrk and server pinned to separate physical cores, tmpfs.
tradeoffs: Serves only a prebuilt CDB archive, so content changes need a rebuild; HTTP/2 is about 6 times slower than its HTTP/1 path (Go net/http), where the author says NGINX is much better; kawipiko used about 1 GiB RAM in the tile run while NGINX used the least; AGPL licence.
caveats: First-party; the per-connection rows are marked 'Last updated in August 2018' and the summary 'December 2021', measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U, i7 4770), the author says the current version is at least 10% more efficient. NGINX is a distro package with an author-tuned config; timeouts and security headers are disabled in the kawipiko run (author says timeouts cost 10-15%). Socket errors and timeouts appear in the 2048 and 16384 connection rows for both servers. The author states the real advantage over NGINX is deployment simplicity, not raw speed, and calls the result 'at least on-par'.
found_via: WebSearch 'static file web server written in Rust OR Zig OR Go "faster than nginx" benchmark wrk requests/sec README comparison h2o lwan' (github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org filter)
why_faster: Content pre-indexed in a CDB archive held in memory with a compact lookup (no per-request file system calls), on Go fasthttp; the README says the advantage grows for many small files accessed in random patterns.

name: monolake
baseline: nginx 1.24.0 (C); build flags not stated
workload: HTTP and HTTPS proxy/serving throughput of the Monolake reference proxy (Rust on the io_uring-based monoio runtime) against nginx, measured as requests per second versus response body size (512 B to 64 KiB) and versus worker threads (1 to 16); load generator, nginx configuration and backend setup are not stated.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the text; four chart images only. Approximate values read from the charts (not stated by the project). HTTPS vs worker threads: 16 threads about 526k req/s vs nginx about 450k (about 1.17x), 8 threads about 359k vs about 334k (about 1.07x). HTTPS vs body size: 512 B about 152k vs about 128k (about 1.19x), 4096 B about 124k vs about 108k (about 1.15x), roughly equal at 8192 B, then nginx ahead at 16384 B (about 55k vs about 59k) and 65536 B (about 20k vs about 23k). Plain HTTP: nginx ahead everywhere, 16 threads about 707k vs about 688k (monolake about 0.97x), 512 B about 186k vs about 168k (monolake about 0.91x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for Monolake or nginx; Monolake needs Rust nightly and Linux 5.1+ for io_uring (docs).
hardware: AWS c6a.8xlarge, AMD EPYC 7R13, 16 cores / 32 threads, 64 GB RAM, Linux 6.1.94-99.176.amzn2023.x86_64 (Amazon Linux 2023.5.20240805), nginx 1.24.0 (README Performance section)

The win is confined to HTTPS with small bodies (and more worker threads); plain HTTP and large HTTPS bodies favour nginx. The nginx build and configuration (workers, logging, TLS library), the workload (static body or proxied backend) and the load generator are not stated, and the TLS stack on each side is unknown. Repository is archived. Tier C: first-party, partial methodology.
found_via: WebSearch 'monolake Rust proxy benchmark vs Nginx throughput cloudwego' surfaced the project; github.com/cloudwego/monolake README Performance section and its four chart PNGs (raw.githubusercontent.com .github/images) opened
why_faster: Thread-per-core io_uring runtime (monoio) with no work stealing, versus nginx's epoll workers; the README gives no explicit explanation for the HTTPS win.

workload: HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy in front of an nginx backend answering '200 OK' with a 2-byte body, wrk -t4 -c100 -d10s keep-alive, two proxy workers each for rproxy and nginx on two pinned cores, loopback.
claimed_speedup: August run: rproxy 323,035 req/s (352 us avg) vs nginx reverse proxy 282,032 (400 us) = 1.15x and HAProxy 266,603 (395 us); June run (median of 3, bare metal): rproxy 189,810 (557 us) vs nginx 153,484 (662 us) = 1.24x. name: Spire
baseline: HAProxy 2.7.3 (C) and Envoy 1.22.8 (C++) reverse proxies; nginx 1.23.3 in the same table is faster than Spire
workload: hey -n 100000 -c 250 GET through each reverse proxy to one backend, docker-compose, proxy and backend limited to 4 CPU cores and 8 GB memory; based on the public NickMRamirez/Proxy-Benchmarks harness.

Single hey run of 100,000 requests lasting about 1 s per proxy, load generator on the same PC, old HAProxy 2.7.3 and Envoy 1.22.8 releases, default or unstated proxy configs, and the README headline 'Exceptional Performance' is not backed by a win over nginx. name: wut-server

The page compares only against nginx and the benchmark harness is not in the repo.
